LESSONS.title: What an inference engine actually does
LESSONS.goal: Explain what happens between sending a prompt and seeing an answer, and which part of that work an inference engine does.
LESSONS.recall: What do you think happens between sending a prompt and seeing the first word?
LESSONS.predict: If two companies serve identical weights, must their speed and running cost be identical?
example: Your team makes three changes to a chatbot. Which part of the system does each change touch?

First the team fine-tunes the model so its replies follow your house style. That changes the learned weights, or a learned adapter on top of them. It belongs to the model, because the same input can now produce a different prediction.
Next the team has the computer process several people’s questions together. The weights can stay exactly as they were. This is an engine decision about how the work is scheduled and executed.

Finally the team adds a sign-in page and sends each request to whichever machine is free. Those jobs belong to the surrounding service. When the chatbot feels slow, knowing which of the three parts changed tells you where to start looking.

questions.prompt: Two teams use exactly the same learned model weights. Could their engines still take different amounts of time and memory to answer?
options: No. Matching weights force identical execution costs.
Yes. The software can organize and execute the same calculations differently.
Only if one team retrains the model.
questions.why: Fixing the learned numbers leaves open how requests are grouped, how memory is managed and how each calculation runs. One engine may avoid repeated work that another engine performs.
questions.hint: Separate learned numbers from how they are executed.
option_feedback: Weights fix what is computed. How requests are grouped, how memory is managed and which kernels run are separate choices.
Correct: the same calculations can be scheduled, batched and executed in different ways, at different cost.
Retraining changes the weights, but the question holds them fixed, and execution cost can still differ.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s public release supports offline inference. What follows?
options: It is already a complete hosted chat service
It cannot allocate any KV memory
A service still needs surrounding components
questions.why: Offline execution keeps local KV state for each request. A hosted service would still need a distributed cache, online routing and the other pieces the README places outside the release.
questions.hint: Local attention state and a fleet cache system are different things.
option_feedback: A hosted chat service also needs routing, sign-in and streaming, which the release leaves out.
Local KV memory is part of running attention at all; what the release omits is a fleet-wide KV-cache service.
Correct: the release covers execution, so routing, a shared cache service and the rest of a service must come from elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Before you accept an optimization, what should you specify first?
options: Workload, output contract and target metrics
Only peak GPU utilization
Only a single impressive tokens/s number
questions.why: You need to know what must stay correct and which measured behavior should improve, on a stated workload.
questions.hint: Ask: faster for whom, doing what?
option_feedback: Correct: an optimization only means something against a workload, a statement of which outputs stay legal, and a target metric.
High utilization can coexist with slow responses or wrong outputs, so it says nothing about the contract.
A single throughput figure omits the workload, the latency each user sees and whether outputs stayed correct.

transfer: A friend asks: “If the model has already been trained, why do we still need an inference engine?” Explain the difference, then name one job the surrounding service does.
Names weights and execution separately
Explains iterative next-token prediction
Names one surrounding service responsibility

Training produced the weights, the learned numbers that determine the model’s calculations. Answering repeats one loop. The engine runs those calculations, chooses a next token, appends it to the text so far and goes again. Along the way it manages memory and coordinates the many requests sharing the hardware. The surrounding service has its own jobs, such as signing users in and sending each request to an available machine.
LESSONS.takeaway: The learned model decides which calculations to do. The engine decides how the computer runs them.

levels.1:
You send a message to a chatbot. There is a pause, and then the answer appears a few words at a time. Somewhere a computer is turning your message into that answer, and a different service running what looks like the same model may do it faster or more cheaply.

To see why, pull apart three things that people often lump together as “the model”: the learned model itself, the software that runs it, and the service you actually talk to.

During training, a computer adjusts a very large collection of numbers until the model gets better at predicting text. Those numbers are the model’s weights. You can think of them as the settings of an enormous machine. Their values decide how information flows through it and which predictions come out.

Training ends with the weights saved to files. Fine-tuning a base model changes those numbers, or adds a smaller learned update on top of them, and so changes how the model behaves.

When the model answers, it uses its weights to score which piece of text could come next. It picks one piece, appends it to the text so far, and makes the next prediction from the longer text. A response is that loop, repeated until it stops.

Running a trained model to make predictions is called inference. In ordinary inference the weights stay fixed. The model’s working state grows as the conversation grows, yet nothing it learned is updated after each word.

Something has to load the weights, reserve memory, decide which requests to work on together, run the calculations and keep track of every unfinished answer. That software is an inference engine. Two engines can run identical weights and still differ in how much memory they use and how long they take.

The service around the engine signs you in and picks which machine receives your request. It also streams the answer back to your screen. Each of those steps adds its own delay, so a fast engine behind a slow service still feels slow.

DeepInfer, the engine DeepSeek has released publicly, is the case study for the rest of the course. Its choices about memory, batching and kernels make more sense once the smaller pieces are in place.
levels.2:
Follow one call through DeepInfer. The public entry point is LLM.generate in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py. For each prompt, _add_request copies the sampling settings, runs the Hugging Face tokenizer’s encode unless you passed token IDs yourself, converts the IDs to a NumPy int32 array and hands them to LLMEngine.add_request. No GPU has done anything yet. The request is now a sequence object waiting in a queue.

_run_engine then loops. While any request is unfinished it calls LLMEngine.step() in deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py and collects whatever outputs that step produced. At the end it turns each request’s token IDs back into text with the tokenizer’s decode. One step advances every scheduled request by one round of the model, so a 500-token answer takes hundreds of steps, interleaved with the steps that serve everyone else. Later lessons show how speculative decoding lets one step emit several tokens for the same request.

Each step has four stages. The scheduler, written in C++ in csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp, picks which sequences run and whether this step processes prompts or extends answers. It also hands out the KV-cache blocks each sequence needs, and it preempts a sequence when blocks run out. _execute_model_async_step passes that plan to the workers. Their execute_model_step in deepinfer/worker/worker.py builds input tensors, runs the forward pass (usually by replaying a captured CUDA graph) and calls the sampler. post_process folds the sampled tokens back into the sequences, marks the finished ones and returns RequestOutput records.

Two jobs before the first step settle most of the memory picture. The workers load the weights, and then profile_run pushes a dummy batch of the largest configured size through the model to measure its peak working memory. In deepinfer/worker/base.py, the memory left for attention state is total memory times gpu_memory_utilization (0.9 by default in EngineArgs), minus that peak, minus a fixed area for per-sequence state. The remainder is divided by the bytes in one cache block. Take an invented 80 GB device holding 40 GB of weights with a 6 GB profiling peak: 72 − 40 − 6 leaves about 26 GB, before the state area, for cached tokens. Raising max_num_seqs or the per-step token budget raises the peak and leaves fewer blocks.

The engine’s interface shows its scope. It takes token IDs plus a SamplingParams object (temperature, top-p, top-k, maximum tokens, a seed, an optional grammar) and returns per-step records holding a token ID, its log probability and speculative-acceptance counts. Everything a chat product does before encoding and after decoding happens outside this loop: converting API requests, applying the chat template, streaming text to a browser. DeepSeek ships that half separately. Its deployment Q&A describes DeepSeek Recipe, which turns Chat Completions, Responses and Messages API requests into token sequences and parses the output back.

The README names the other missing pieces. The release runs offline inference and lists, as required for a full service but not included, a KV cache system, disaggregated vision-encoder, prefill and decode deployment, and load balancing across data-parallel replicas. The code shows where they would attach. EngineType in deepinfer/engine/engine_type.py has NORMAL, PROMPT (prefill only) and COMPLETION (decode only), and the scheduler refuses to let a decode-only engine recompute a preempted request because that engine has no way to run a prompt. An offline run uses NORMAL, a single engine doing both kinds of work.

Symptoms map onto these layers. A mismatched tokenizer produces valid-looking IDs the weights were never trained on, which is why deepinfer/hugging_face/tokenizer.py refuses to start unless the begin, end and padding tokens sit at IDs 0, 1 and 2. Too little memory headroom fails at startup with “No available memory for the cache blocks” or shows up later as preemption. A scheduling choice changes latency without changing any computed number. Each one calls for a different fix, so find the layer that produced a symptom before you change anything.
levels.3:
DeepInfer’s README says it “was originally built primarily on vLLM”, with ideas from SGLang and NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM, and many of its files still carry a “Derived from vLLM” header. That lineage is the recent history of the field. Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues’ Orca (OSDI 2022) introduced iteration-level scheduling, letting requests join and leave a running batch at every step. Woosuk Kwon and colleagues’ PagedAttention paper (SOSP 2023), the basis of vLLM, stored attention state in fixed-size blocks so memory was no longer reserved for each request’s worst case. It reported 2–4× the throughput of the systems it compared against, at the same latency. Lianmin Zheng and colleagues’ SGLang added RadixAttention, a prefix tree that lets requests sharing a prompt prefix reuse its cached state. Most of what a modern engine does descends from these three ideas plus fast kernels.

The frontier has since moved from the single engine to the fleet. DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A describes the production system around DeepInfer as disaggregated. Vision encoders, prefill machines (ordinary 8-GPU nodes) and decode groups of 64–128 GPUs are each scaled separately, and a dedicated storage cluster on DeepSeek’s 3FS file system retains KV caches for days so that a returning conversation can skip most of its prefill. Yinmin Zhong and colleagues’ DistServe and Pratyush Patel and colleagues’ Splitwise, both from 2024, made the research case for running prefill and decode on separate machines. Moonshot AI’s Mooncake built a production service around a disaggregated KV store. The open release is the engine of such a system, minus the cache and routing components the Q&A says are tied to internal infrastructure.

Read the production figures for what they are. The Q&A reports that one cluster serves 155 trillion tokens a day and earns US$38 per GPU-hour at off-peak prices. These are author-reported, with no published workload trace, so no outsider can reproduce them. The README’s benchmark plots are on firmer ground: they come with a sweep script, examples/sweep/run_sweep.sh, and they are Pareto curves of output throughput against per-user speed, measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode. A curve is the honest unit of comparison, because any engine can buy throughput with latency by enlarging its batches, and a single peak figure hides which trade was made.

The harder question is what “the same model” means after an engine change. Three contracts are in use, and DeepInfer exhibits all of them. Bitwise equivalence: with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, verification lengths fixed and a fixed seq_seed, the README promises identical outputs whatever else shares the batch, and tests/models/test_batch_invariant.py compares batched runs with single runs. Distributional equivalence: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias, and independently Charlie Chen and colleagues at DeepMind, showed in 2023 that speculative sampling can change which token a given random draw yields while leaving the probability of every output unchanged. Deliberate approximation: the Q&A says SWA bounded replay recomputes only the last 128 tokens and “yields an approximate SWA KV cache”, and FP8 or FP4 storage rounds every value it holds.

Each contract can be legitimate, and each needs a different test. Bitwise claims are checked by exact comparison. Distributional claims need many samples or a proof about the acceptance rule. Approximations need task-level evaluation, because no single tolerance on logits says whether answers got worse. Horace He, writing for Thinking Machines Lab in 2025, argued that most run-to-run variation in served models comes from kernels whose arithmetic order changes with batch size, so the same prompt gets slightly different scores depending on who else is on the server. A team that skips naming the contract cannot tell such variation from a real bug.

Several problems remain open. MLPerf Inference (Vijay Janapa Reddi and colleagues, 2020) standardized scenarios such as Offline and Server with latency bounds, but chat and agent traffic, with long shared prefixes and cache reuse across days, is poorly represented in public traces. There is no agreed test for “approximately the same model” short of task evaluations, which are noisy and expensive to run. And when a fleet-level gain depends on routing, cache hit rate and the ratio of prefill to decode machines (the Q&A puts it near 1:1), engine microbenchmarks cannot isolate it. Ask every claim which workload, which contract, which metric and which hardware it was measured on.

LESSONS.title: The math you need, without the fog
LESSONS.goal: Read the small amount of arithmetic and notation that inference explanations rely on.
LESSONS.recall: What is a weight, and what changes during inference?
LESSONS.predict: Does a vector with 4 entries multiplied by a 4×6 matrix produce 4 numbers or 6?
example: A weight table has 10 rows and 20 columns, and each number takes two bytes. How much storage does the table need, and how long does it take to move?
Count the entries first: 10 × 20 = 200 numbers. The shape alone tells you how many values exist, without looking at any of them.
Multiply by the storage per entry: 200 × 2 = 400 bytes. That is the raw numbers only. A program may need more memory for bookkeeping and temporary results.

Now send those 400 bytes over a link rated at 100 bytes per second. Even with no overhead the transfer takes four seconds, because bytes divided by bytes per second leaves seconds. The same reasoning applies later to billions of model weights.

questions.prompt: X has shape [8,4] and W has shape [4,6]. What shape is XW?
questions.why: The shared inner dimension 4 is summed away and the outer dimensions remain, so XW has 8 rows and 6 columns.
questions.hint: Track tokens on rows and output features on columns.
option_feedback: Correct: the shared inner dimension 4 is summed away, leaving the 8 rows of X and the 6 columns of W.
This keeps the inner dimension, which is exactly the one the multiplication combines.
[6,8] is the shape of the transpose, (XW)ᵀ. XW keeps the rows of X first.

questions.prompt: A billion parameters at 2 bytes each need roughly how much memory?
options: 2 MB
2 GB for weights alone
2 GB for the entire service including every cache
questions.why: Parameter count times bytes per parameter gives the storage for the weights. The running footprint also includes caches, activations and runtime overhead.
questions.hint: What memory has the calculation omitted?
option_feedback: Off by a factor of a thousand: 10⁹ × 2 bytes is 2 × 10⁹ bytes, while 2 MB is 2 × 10⁶ bytes.
Correct: 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 2 × 10⁹ bytes, about 2 GB, and that covers the weights only.
The arithmetic gives 2 GB, but it counts weights only. Caches and working memory come on top.

transfer: Explain the difference between how much memory a device has and how quickly it can move data. Use a small example.
Separates capacity from transfer rate
Names bytes/s as bandwidth
Explains why both constrain inference

Capacity is how much data fits at once. Bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second. A table of 200 numbers at two bytes each needs 400 bytes of raw storage. Over a link that moves 100 bytes per second, moving it takes at least four seconds. Having room to store the table does nothing to make that transfer faster.
LESSONS.takeaway: A tensor’s shape tells you how its numbers are arranged. The units tell you what a calculation measures.

levels.1:
Explanations of inference tend to jump straight to words like “tensor” and “matrix multiplication”. The ideas underneath are concrete enough to work through on paper, so that is where to start.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as [2, 3]. A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers, with rows and columns. Tensor is the general name for an array organized along any number of directions. A vector has one direction and a matrix has two.

Suppose you have four requests, each ten text positions long, and you represent every position with six numbers. You can store all of it in a tensor of shape [4, 10, 6]. The shape records how many requests, positions and features there are. It says nothing about the values stored inside.

That gap matters when you debug. Two tensors can share a shape and hold completely different values, so a passing shape check rules out some mistakes and proves nothing about whether the model computed the right answer.

The expression [2, 3] · [4, 5] asks you to multiply matching entries and add the results: 2 × 4 + 3 × 5 = 23. That is a dot product. Matrix multiplication performs many dot products at once, and inside a model a learned matrix uses them to turn one set of features into another.

Papers write shapes with symbols such as [B, d], where B might be the number of positions being processed and d the number of features per position. Multiplying by a matrix of shape [d, h] gives [B, h]. The shared d is the dimension that gets summed away.

Inference arithmetic also keeps asking how many bytes fit and how long they take to move. If each stored number takes two bytes, a billion numbers take about two billion bytes, which is two decimal gigabytes. That covers those numbers only. Any other working memory comes on top.

A device that moves one hundred gigabytes per second needs at least a hundredth of a second, ten milliseconds, to move one gigabyte. Capacity is about what fits and bandwidth is about how fast it moves. Later lessons use that difference to explain why very fast hardware sometimes spends its time waiting.
levels.2:
Shapes in a real engine follow one convention more often than any other: activations are stored row-major as [tokens, features], and a weight that maps d inputs to h outputs is stored as [h, d], one row per output. DeepInfer’s ReplicatedLinear in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/linear.py documents its weight as (output_size, input_size), and its matrix routine is called bf16_gemm_nt: the first operand is used as stored (N, “normal”) and the second is transposed (T). The logits computation in sampler_utils.get_logits is a clean example. Hidden states [tokens, d] times an embedding matrix stored as [vocab, d] gives logits [tokens, vocab], written to a float32 buffer.

To count work, treat each multiply-add as two floating-point operations. For X[B,d] times a weight mapping d to h, every one of the B×h outputs sums d products, so the product costs about 2Bdh FLOPs. Summed over a whole model, that gives the familiar estimate from Jared Kaplan and colleagues’ 2020 scaling-law paper: a forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs per token for N parameters, plus an attention term that grows with context length. DeepInfer bakes the same convention into csrc/engine/flops_estimator.hpp, which counts major contractions at two FLOPs per multiply-add and leaves out small arithmetic such as normalizations, in order to report utilization.

Bytes depend on the number format. A float32 value takes 4 bytes. BF16 takes 2: it keeps float32’s 8 exponent bits, so its range is the same, and keeps only 7 fraction bits, about three significant decimal digits. FP8 E4M3 takes 1 byte with 4 exponent and 3 fraction bits, and its largest finite value is 448. FP4 E2M1 takes half a byte and can represent only 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6, with a sign. Formats this narrow work only with block scaling: a group of values shares one scale factor, and each stored number is a small multiple of it.

DeepInfer’s KV-cache format shows the arithmetic. V41_FORMAT in tilelang_ops/cache_common.py stores, for each token and layer, 512 numbers in E4M3 plus one scale per 32 numbers in UE8M0, an unsigned 8-bit exponent that encodes a power of two. That is 512 × 1 + (512 / 32) × 1 = 528 bytes. The same 512 numbers in BF16 would take 1,024 bytes. The FP4 variant, V41_FP4_FORMAT, packs two values per byte with one E4M3 scale per 16: 256 + 32 = 288 bytes. Multiply by layers and tokens to get a request’s footprint, and remember that the weights, the activation peak and the runtime come on top.

Units decide whether an estimate is right. GB is 10⁹ bytes and GiB is 2³⁰, about 7% more. Capacity is bytes and bandwidth is bytes per second, so bytes divided by bandwidth is a time. A billion parameters at 2 bytes each are 2 × 10⁹ bytes, 2 GB, which is the weights alone. One float32 row of logits over a 129,280-entry vocabulary (the size implied by DeepInfer’s tokenizer, whose extra tokens start at ID 129,280) is 129,280 × 4 = 517,120 bytes, so a step that scores 256 positions writes about 132 MB of logits before any sampling.

Probabilities are handled in log space. Multiplying many probabilities below one quickly underflows, while adding their logarithms does not, since log(p₁p₂) = log p₁ + log p₂. A model’s quality on known text is reported as average negative log probability per token, and its exponential is perplexity. examples/offline_inference.py computes exactly that for each generated answer: exp(−sum(logps) / len(logps)). Softmax is computed stably by subtracting the largest logit before exponentiating, which leaves the result unchanged because the shift cancels between numerator and denominator.

LESSONS.title: Tokens, logits and choosing what comes next
LESSONS.goal: Follow the repeated choices that turn a prompt into a generated response.
LESSONS.recall: How is a probability different from an arbitrary numerical score?
LESSONS.predict: If you raise temperature, do you add knowledge or change how the same scores are sampled?
example: The model gives three possible next tokens probabilities of 66.5%, 24.5% and 9%. What happens next?
Under greedy decoding the engine picks the first token, because 66.5% is the largest probability. No random draw is needed.

Under sampling the first token is still the most likely, but either of the others can be drawn. Seeing the second token, which has a 24.5% chance, is no evidence on its own that the engine made a mistake.

Whichever token is chosen joins the sequence, and the next prediction uses the updated sequence. Raising the temperature would reshape the distribution for this choice and leave the learned weights untouched.

questions.prompt: What does temperature change?
options: The learned weights
The next-token sampling distribution
The tokenizer vocabulary
questions.why: Temperature rescales the logits at sampling time, after the model has computed them. The weights and the vocabulary stay as they were.
questions.hint: Which part happens after the model computes its scores?
option_feedback: Temperature is applied after the model has produced its scores, and the weights that produced them stay fixed.
Correct: dividing the logits by T reshapes the probabilities used to pick the next token.
The vocabulary is fixed by the tokenizer. Temperature only changes how likely each existing token is to be picked.

questions.prompt: Why can’t ordinary autoregressive generation choose 100 unknown future tokens independently in one step?
options: Each choice conditions later predictions
All GPUs forbid matrices with 100 rows
Tokenization is random
questions.why: Each future conditional distribution depends on the tokens generated before it. Speculative decoding works around this by proposing several candidates and then verifying them.
questions.hint: Known text and unknown text have different dependencies.
option_feedback: Correct: the distribution for each token depends on which tokens were chosen before it, so later choices cannot be made first.
GPUs routinely multiply matrices with far more than 100 rows. The limit comes from the dependency between tokens.
Tokenization is deterministic for a given tokenizer. Randomness enters only at sampling.

questions.prompt: Two engines diverge on the 20th generated token. A useful next check is…
options: Only compare the final paragraphs
Teacher-force the same prefixes and compare logits
Increase temperature until the text looks similar
questions.why: Once two outputs diverge, every later token is conditioned on a different history. Teacher forcing keeps the history identical, so any remaining difference in logits comes from the computation itself.
questions.hint: Keep the input to the comparison identical.
option_feedback: The final paragraphs mix every earlier difference together and cannot show where the first disagreement began.
Correct: feeding both engines the same prefixes lets you compare their scores before different histories confound the comparison.
Raising temperature buries the disagreement under more randomness and makes the outputs harder to compare.

transfer: Explain how a model goes from a prompt to a longer answer. Include where choosing the next token happens.
Describes turning text into token IDs
Explains scoring, choosing, and appending a next token
Explains why the chosen token affects the next prediction

The tokenizer turns the prompt into token IDs. The model computes a score for every possible next token, and the engine’s selection rule picks one. That token is appended before the next prediction, so each choice shapes the input to the next step. The tokenizer and stop markers have to match what the model was trained with. Changing temperature changes which tokens get picked, while the learned weights stay the same.
LESSONS.takeaway: Generation repeatedly scores possible next tokens, chooses one, and adds it to the text so far.

levels.1:
Before the model runs, a piece of software called the tokenizer breaks your text into smaller pieces and gives each one an integer. The pieces are tokens and the integers are token IDs.

A token can be a common word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a special marker. An invented tokenizer might split “unhelpful” into “un”, “help” and “ful”. Real tokenizers each make their own choices, and the split for any given word depends on which one you use.

So a limit of a thousand tokens is a different limit from a thousand words. It is also why a fine-tuned model has to be loaded with its own tokenizer, since its weights were learned against those particular token IDs.

Suppose the input ends with “The sky is”. The model produces a score for every token it could place next, and some continuations score far higher than others. These raw scores are called logits. They are not probabilities yet, and they need not add up to one.

A function called softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Each probability says how likely one choice is, and across all the candidate tokens they sum to one.

The engine still has to pick. It can take the highest-scoring token every time, which is called greedy decoding. Or it can draw a token at random according to the probabilities, in which case a less likely token is sometimes chosen, just as a coin that lands heads 70% of the time still lands tails now and then.

Temperature controls how concentrated those probabilities are. A low temperature gives the top choices more of the probability, and a high temperature spreads it out. Either way the model’s knowledge is untouched. Only the rule for choosing has changed.

Once a token is chosen, the engine appends it to the sequence and the model scores what could follow the longer text. Choosing “blue” puts the model in a different situation from choosing “clear”, so every later prediction can differ.

The engine repeats this cycle of scoring, choosing and appending until it reaches a stopping condition. The answer on your screen is the trail of those choices, assembled one token at a time.
levels.2:
Start with the formula. For logits z over the vocabulary and temperature T > 0, pᵢ = exp(zᵢ/T) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ/T). Take three candidates with logits 2, 1 and 0. At T = 1 the exponentials are 7.39, 2.72 and 1, which sum to 11.11, so the probabilities are 66.5%, 24.5% and 9.0%. At T = 0.5 the scaled logits are 4, 2 and 0, and the probabilities become 86.7%, 11.7% and 1.6%. At T = 2 they flatten to 50.6%, 30.7% and 18.6%. The model produced the same three logits each time. Only the selection step changed.

In DeepInfer the logits come from get_logits in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/sampler_utils.py, which multiplies the final hidden states by the embedding matrix into a float32 tensor of shape [tokens, vocab]. The Sampler in sampler.py first gathers only the rows that need a choice. During a prompt pass that means the last prompt position of each request; the prompt’s other positions already have known next tokens.

The selection pipeline lives in process_sampling and tilelang_ops/fused_sample.py, whose PyTorch reference, fused_sample_ref, spells out the order. If DEEPINFER_SAMPLER_FORCE_TOPK is set (the offline example uses 4,096), only the 4,096 highest logits survive. The survivors are divided by T. Top-p then removes every candidate whose preceding cumulative probability already exceeds p. Top-k removes everything ranked below k. A log-softmax renormalizes what is left. With the T = 1 numbers above and p = 0.9, the first token is kept, and the second is kept because the mass before it, 0.665, is below 0.9. The third is removed because 0.91 precedes it. Applied in a different order, the same settings can keep a different set, so record the engine’s order when comparing outputs.

Greedy decoding has no separate code path here. SamplingParams in deepinfer/sampling_params.py raises any temperature below 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁵ and switches off top-p and top-k. At that temperature a logit gap of 0.01 becomes a factor of e¹⁰⁰⁰ in probability, so the result is the argmax except for exact ties.

The random draw is built to be reproducible. random_sampling_ref in tilelang_ops/random_sampling.py hashes the request’s 64-bit seq_seed together with the token’s position through a SplitMix64 mixer into a uniform number u between 0 and 1. It then returns the first token whose cumulative probability, summed in float64, exceeds u times the total. This is inverse-CDF sampling. Because u depends only on the seed and position, the draw for a request does not change with batch size or row order. If you pass no seed, SamplingParams picks a random one, and runs will differ.

Stopping is also a sampling-time rule. A request ends when it emits the end-of-sequence token (ID 1 for this tokenizer) unless ignore_eos is set, or when it reaches max_tokens, which defaults to 16. The prefill path can forbid the end token for the first output (first_n_token_no_eos) by setting its logit to −∞ before sampling. Structured outputs work the same way at larger scale: a grammar matcher produces a bitmask of legal tokens each step, and the sampler sets the logits of all other tokens to −∞.

None of this lifts the sequential dependency. A causal model factors a sequence’s probability as P(x₁…xₙ) = Πₜ P(xₜ | x<ₜ), so the distribution for position t is not even defined until the tokens before it are chosen. Known prompt tokens can be scored in one pass. Unknown tokens must be chosen in order, or proposed in bulk and then checked, which is the move speculative decoding makes.
levels.3:
Tokenizers are learned compressors with consequences downstream. Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch adapted byte-pair encoding, a 1994 compression method by Philip Gage, to neural translation in 2016: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols until the vocabulary reaches a target size. OpenAI’s GPT-2 (Alec Radford and colleagues, 2019) ran the merges over bytes, so any string can be encoded. Taku Kudo and John Richardson’s SentencePiece made the process language-independent. Each choice fixes what the model can see. Jessica Rumbelow and Matthew Watkins’ 2023 “SolidGoldMagikarp” investigation found vocabulary entries that almost never appeared in training and made models behave erratically. Aleksandar Petrov and colleagues showed the same text costs very different numbers of tokens in different languages, which changes price and effective context length per language.

Boundaries cause quieter failures. If a prompt ends with a space or half a word, the most natural continuation may be a token that begins with that space, which the prompt has already used up. Microsoft’s Guidance library introduced “token healing” to back up one token and constrain the next choice to match. Control tokens are a security boundary too. DeepSeek’s Q&A says DeepSeek Recipe encodes a literal <｜User｜> typed by a user as ordinary text tokens, and recognizes the end-of-reasoning marker only by its token ID, so text cannot impersonate a control token. A comparison between engines is meaningful only once the token IDs match exactly.

Sampling rules are judged empirically, and the evidence is softer than the formulas. Angela Fan, Mike Lewis and Yann Dauphin used top-k sampling for story generation in 2018. Ari Holtzman and colleagues’ 2020 paper on neural text degeneration showed that maximizing likelihood produces repetitive text and proposed nucleus (top-p) sampling, supported by human judgments and distributional statistics. Minh Nguyen and colleagues proposed min-p in 2024, which scales the cutoff by the top token’s probability. These comparisons depend on the temperature, the task and who judges, so a sampling setting tuned on one model rarely transfers unchanged to another.

Some engine shortcuts change the distribution itself. DeepInfer’s force_topk gives zero probability to every token outside the top 4,096. That mass is usually tiny, but it is not zero, and at high temperature it grows. tests/models/test_kl.py admits the consequence: it refuses a nonzero tolerance on divergence while force_topk is on, because a token with zero probability in one distribution and positive probability in the other makes the KL divergence infinite. Grammar masks change the distribution too. Kanghee Park and colleagues showed in 2024 that masking token by token does not sample from the model’s distribution restricted to grammatical outputs. Yixin Dong and colleagues’ XGrammar, whose masks DeepInfer applies, and Brandon Willard and Rémi Louf’s Outlines made masking fast. Being fast leaves this bias in place.

Reproducibility needs more than a seed. A seed fixes the random draws, yet the logits can still shift by a rounding error when a kernel sums in a different order, for example because the batch grew. Horace He’s 2025 essay for Thinking Machines Lab traced most run-to-run nondeterminism in served models to this lack of batch invariance. DeepInfer addresses both halves. Its sampler keys the random number to (seed, position), and DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 makes kernels compute the same result whatever else is in the batch. The README still requires DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 for deterministic sampling, because confidence-scheduled verification chooses how many draft tokens to check from the current load, and that choice changes which random draws are consumed.

When two engines diverge, compare scores, not prose. Teacher forcing feeds both the same continuation and compares log probabilities at identical prefixes. DeepInfer supports it through golden_token_ids in SamplingParams. In the sampler, _update_golden_tokens replaces each sampled token with the golden one while still recording the model’s log probability for it. The first position where the two engines’ log probabilities differ beyond rounding noise marks where to look. Once histories diverge, every later difference is confounded by the different prefix.

LESSONS.title: A transformer pass and its KV cache
LESSONS.goal: Explain how a new token uses earlier text, and what the engine remembers to avoid repeating work.
LESSONS.recall: What makes a generated token depend on earlier ones?
LESSONS.predict: If you retain old keys and values, do you still need to compare a new query with them?
example: The prompt contains tokens A, B and C, and the engine is now processing token D. What can it reuse?
The engine already holds keys and values for A, B and C at every layer. They stay in this request’s cache, and D’s arrival is no reason to rebuild them.

Compute D’s query, key and value. D’s query is compared with every visible key, including D’s own, and the matching values are mixed into D’s attention result. The engine reads the earlier cache to do this.

Append D’s key and value so the next position can use them. If the engine reads another request’s cache by mistake, or writes D into the wrong slot, the result can be wrong even though the cache has the expected length.

questions.prompt: What does a KV cache mainly save?
options: Recomputing earlier positions’ keys and values
All future attention calculations
The need for model weights
questions.why: Each new query still attends to the cached context. What the cache saves is rebuilding the earlier positions’ keys and values at every step.
questions.hint: Saved computation does not mean zero reads.
option_feedback: Correct: keys and values for earlier positions are computed once and read again, instead of being recomputed.
Each new query still has to attend over the cached keys and values. The cache saves recomputation, and the reads remain.
The cache holds per-request intermediate results. The weights are still needed to compute every new position.

questions.prompt: Can a text token reuse the same KV vector in any sentence?
options: Yes, keys depend only on spelling
No, hidden states depend on context and position
Only if temperature is zero
questions.why: Later-layer representations reflect the preceding tokens and the token’s position, so a key or value is tied to one history.
questions.hint: The token embedding is only the start of the computation.
option_feedback: Spelling fixes only the token’s embedding. Keys and values at later layers depend on the preceding text and the position.
Correct: hidden states reflect the preceding tokens and the position, so the same token gets different keys and values in different contexts.
Temperature affects only how the next token is chosen and has no effect on the keys and values the layers compute.

questions.prompt: Which check most directly tests a KV cache?
options: Generated output looks fluent
Full-forward and incremental logits agree on the same prefixes
The cache has the expected Python type
questions.why: Numerical agreement across positions tests the actual computation the cache is meant to reproduce.
questions.hint: Compare a reference computation, not the appearance of the result.
option_feedback: Fluent text can hide a subtly wrong cache, because the model may still produce plausible words from slightly wrong scores.
Correct: if incremental and full-forward logits match at every prefix, the cache reproduces the computation it replaces.
A correct Python type says nothing about whether the stored values are the right ones.

transfer: Walk through what the engine does when one new token arrives. What does it calculate, and what can it reuse?
Computes a new query/key/value
Uses past keys and values
Appends request-specific state

The new position needs its own query, key and value. Its query is compared with the visible keys to decide how to mix the matching values. Keys and values for earlier positions come from this request’s cache and are not recalculated. The engine then appends the new key and value to that cache. It still reads the earlier state on every step, and that state has to come from the correct history.
LESSONS.takeaway: The engine saves earlier attention state so each new token can use it without rebuilding it.

levels.1:
Read “The trophy would not fit in the suitcase because it was too large.” To decide what “it” refers to, you have to use words elsewhere in the sentence. A model faces the same problem, so it needs a way for the representation at one position to draw on information from other positions.

Attention is the mechanism transformers use for this. The model first represents each token as a list of numbers called an embedding. It then transforms and mixes those lists through a stack of layers, each of which is one stage of the calculation.

At each position, a layer computes three lists of numbers. The query is compared with the keys of every visible position to produce matching scores, and those scores decide how much of each position’s value goes into a weighted mixture. A position with a high score contributes more.

The names sound human, yet nothing is asking a literal question or looking anything up in a dictionary. Queries, keys and values are lists of numbers produced by multiplying by learned matrices. The names describe the role each list plays in the calculation.

A model trained to continue text must never see the token it is supposed to predict. A causal mask enforces this by blocking attention to later positions. As a result, the computation for an earlier position stays the same when a new token is appended.

That stability is an opportunity. Say the engine has processed “The sky is” and is working on the next token. It has already computed keys and values for the earlier positions, so it can keep them in memory and skip computing them again.

The saved state is a KV cache, K for keys and V for values. The new position still needs its own calculations, and its query still reads the saved keys and values. Caching removes repeated work, while the earlier context still has to be read on every step.

“Bank” in a sentence about a river ends up with a different representation from “bank” in a sentence about money, because deeper layers fold in context. A cached key or value therefore cannot in general be reused just because the same token ID shows up somewhere else.

That gives the engine a concrete job. It has to keep the right state for each request, use it in the right order and release it once it is no longer needed. Get this wrong and the predictions can be wrong while every array still has a perfectly valid shape.
levels.2:
Write a layer with shapes. For one head with head size dₕ, Q = XW_q, K = XW_k, V = XW_v, each [tokens, dₕ]. The output is softmax(QKᵀ/√dₕ + M)V, where M holds 0 for visible pairs and −∞ for hidden ones, so hidden pairs get zero weight. The scaling by √dₕ keeps dot products from growing with head size. Many heads run in parallel with their own projections, and an output projection mixes their results. Positions enter through rotary embeddings (RoPE, from Jianlin Su and colleagues’ 2021 RoFormer), which rotate each query and key by an angle set by its position before the dot product. A cached key is therefore already rotated for its own position.

Count what a cache costs. Conventional multi-head attention stores a key and a value per head per layer: 2 × heads × dₕ × bytes per token per layer. For an invented model with 32 layers and 32 heads of size 128 in BF16, that is 2 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 16,384 bytes per layer, 512 KiB per token across layers, and 2 GiB for a single 4,096-token conversation. Decode reads all of it at every step. The cache, not the arithmetic, is usually what limits how many conversations fit on a device.

DeepInfer’s V4.1 attention, in deepinfer/model_executor/models/v4_modules/attn.py, attacks that number in several ways at once. All heads share one 512-number latent per token, so the prefill kernel receives keys shaped [total_k, 1, head_dim] rather than one per head. The latent is stored in FP8 with block scales, 528 bytes per token per layer, about 31 times smaller than the 16 KiB example. Some layers keep only a sliding window of recent tokens. Others keep a compressed cache in which each entry summarizes several tokens (kv_compress_ratio), and a small indexer in index_attn.py scores those entries and passes each query only the top-scoring ones. The visible set is therefore a list of indices per query, which generalizes the triangular mask.

The two phases call different kernels in deepinfer/model_executor/layers/attention_backend.py. In prefill, forward assembles one buffer of keys from three parts, the cached window, the window keys computed in this pass and compressed entries loaded from the paged cache, and calls prefill_attn_varlen_sparse. “Varlen” means sequences of different lengths are packed end to end in one [total_q, heads, dim] tensor rather than padded to a common length. In decode, decode_mla_mqa_sparse reads directly from the paged cache, laid out [num_blocks, block_size, 1, bytes_per_token] as raw bytes, using per-query index lists.

Writing the cache is where order bugs live. New keys pass through one fused kernel, fused_norm_rope_hadamard_cast_store_kvcache, which normalizes, applies RoPE, rotates, casts to FP8 and stores. Store slots come from a slot mapping that translates each token position to a block and an offset within it. A comment in attn.py states a real hazard: the window’s store slots can overlap the ranges just loaded, so prefill must store only after the cache load. Reverse the two and the kernel reads the values it has just overwritten. Every shape stays correct and the output is wrong.

A cache entry is a function of the layer, the position and every token before it. Two requests that share a prompt prefix can share those entries. That is the basis of prefix caching, and DeepInfer’s scheduler clones block tables when a request forks. The same token ID at a different position, or after different text, gets a different entry.
levels.3:
The history of attention in inference is mostly a history of shrinking the cache. Noam Shazeer’s 2019 multi-query attention let all heads share one key and value, cutting the cache by the head count at some cost in quality. Joshua Ainslie and colleagues’ grouped-query attention (2023) shared one key-value pair per group of heads and showed that existing models could be converted with a little extra training. DeepSeek-V2 (2024) introduced multi-head latent attention, which compresses keys and values into a low-rank latent and reconstructs per-head views from it. The paper reported a 93.3% smaller KV cache and up to 5.76× the generation throughput of DeepSeek 67B. DeepInfer’s single shared latent per token descends from that design, though the V2 paper is not a specification of V4.1.

A second line limits which tokens a query can see. Iz Beltagy and colleagues’ Longformer (2020) and later Mistral 7B used sliding windows. Guangxuan Xiao and colleagues’ StreamingLLM (2023) found that models put large attention weight on the first few tokens whatever they contain, and that windowed attention breaks unless those “sinks” are kept. DeepInfer passes a learned per-head attn_sink parameter to its FlashMLA kernels for the same reason. Learned selection followed. Jingyang Yuan and colleagues’ Native Sparse Attention (2025) trained compression and selection into the model. DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp introduced DeepSeek Sparse Attention, in which a lightweight indexer picks the top-k past entries for each query. DeepInfer’s index_attn.py describes its indexer as computing relu(q @ k) * weights scores and selecting the top-k blocks.

A third line shares the cache across layers. Yutao Sun and colleagues’ You Only Cache Once (2024) let later layers cross-attend to keys and values produced once by earlier layers. DeepInfer’s yoco.py and cross_layer.py use producer and consumer layers in this spirit, and the deployment Q&A adds an approximation on top: instead of rebuilding a consumer layer’s window over the last 2,560 tokens, prefill replays only the last 128, which the authors say nearly halves prefill computation. The result is used for decoding only and never enters the shared prefix cache. That is a sensible guard, since a cached approximation would otherwise be reused as if exact.

Competing approaches drop the growing cache altogether. Albert Gu and Tri Dao’s Mamba (2023) carries a fixed-size recurrent state, so memory does not grow with context, and several labs now mix such layers with attention layers. Their weakness is the mirror image of attention’s: a fixed state must decide in advance what to forget, while a full cache can look anything up again.

How do we know any of these trade-offs is acceptable? The memory saving is exact arithmetic. The quality cost is not, and it is measured badly. A model can retrieve one planted fact from a long document while failing at tasks that combine many facts. Cheng-Ping Hsieh and colleagues’ RULER benchmark (2024) found that many models claiming long contexts degraded well before their advertised length. Compression, sparsity, windows and replay each discard information in a different way, and their errors can compound over a long generation. A short evaluation will not show that.

The engine-level check is sharper than any benchmark. tests/models/test_kl.py runs the same image-and-text inputs two ways, once step by step through decode and once as a single full prefill over the prompt plus the golden continuation, and compares the log probabilities at every position. The configured case sets the allowed KL divergence to zero, so incremental decoding must reproduce the full pass exactly. A test like this catches a cache written to the wrong slot, a misaligned position or a stale window, all of which still yield fluent text. It cannot catch an approximation that both paths share, which is why the bounded replay result is kept out of the comparison path and out of the prefix cache. Open questions include how to bound quality loss from approximate caches over long agent sessions, and how to give reused prefixes from days-old caches the same guarantees as fresh ones.

LESSONS.title: Prefill, decode and what users feel
LESSONS.goal: Separate the wait before an answer starts from the speed at which it continues.
LESSONS.recall: Why are known prompt tokens different from unknown generated tokens?
LESSONS.predict: A huge prompt gives a long initial pause but fast streaming. Which phase should you investigate first?
example: The first token arrives after 400 milliseconds. Nine more tokens arrive with 50 milliseconds between them. When is the answer complete?
The first token arrives at 400 milliseconds, and that wait is counted once. Depending on where the clock started, it may include queueing, input preparation and model execution.
Nine gaps follow the first token. Nine times 50 milliseconds is 450 milliseconds, all of it spent continuing the answer.
Add the two parts: 400 + 450 = 850 milliseconds. Shortening the initial wait and shortening every later gap change different parts of that total.

questions.prompt: An answer begins after a long pause and then streams quickly. Which metric should you look at first?
options: TTFT
Only final token count
Training loss
questions.why: The symptom concerns the time until the first token, so TTFT is the measurement that matches it. The quick streaming suggests decode is not the problem.
questions.hint: Match the metric to the experience.
option_feedback: Correct: the symptom is the wait before the first token, which is exactly what TTFT measures.
The token count says how long the answer is, and nothing about when its first token arrived.
Training loss describes how well the model learned. It says nothing about serving delay.

questions.prompt: 100 requests each receive 10 tokens/s. What is the aggregate output rate?
options: 10 tokens/s
100 tokens/s
1,000 tokens/s
questions.why: Aggregate throughput sums the per-request rates: 100 × 10 = 1,000 tokens/s. Each user still sees only 10 tokens/s.
questions.hint: Per-user and fleet metrics use different denominators.
option_feedback: 10 tokens/s is the per-request rate. The aggregate adds up all 100 requests.
100 tokens/s counts one token per second per request, when each request gets ten.
Correct: 100 requests × 10 tokens/s each = 1,000 tokens/s across the system.

questions.prompt: Offline throughput improves while online p99 worsens. Is that possible?
options: No, throughput determines all latency
Yes, batching or queueing can raise tail latency
Only if weights changed
questions.why: An offline benchmark measures total work with every request present from the start. Online, requests arrive over time and may wait to join a batch, so the slowest ones can get slower.
questions.hint: What happens to a request waiting to join work?
option_feedback: Throughput measures total work per second. It does not determine how long any single request waits.
Correct: larger batches can raise total throughput while requests waiting to join them see longer tail latency.
The weights affect what is computed. Scheduling alone can trade tail latency for throughput.

transfer: Someone says their chatbot is slow. What would you ask and measure before choosing a fix?
Separates initial delay and streaming gaps
Includes queueing/preprocessing
Requests workload and percentile measurements

I would first ask whether the delay comes before the first token or between later tokens. The initial wait can include queueing, input preparation and prompt processing. Later gaps point at continued generation, though delivery can matter there too. I would time those stages under the person’s real input lengths and request load, and look at the slow requests as well as the average. That tells me where to start.
LESSONS.takeaway: Processing the known prompt and generating the unknown continuation are different kinds of work.

activity.title: Measure the wait a user actually sees.
activity.intro: A request waits in a queue for 120 milliseconds. Input preparation, prompt processing, and first-token delivery take another 180 milliseconds. The answer contains five output tokens, with 40 milliseconds between successive tokens. Use the moment the request was submitted as time zero.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the first output token arrives?
fields.why: The initial wait includes both the queue and the work before first delivery: 120 + 180 = 300 milliseconds.

fields.label: How many milliseconds until the fifth and final output token arrives?
fields.why: After the first token there are four gaps, not five: 300 + 4 × 40 = 460 milliseconds.

activity.conclusion: A timer that runs only inside the engine can miss the queue and the delivery. Whenever you measure your own model, save the clock boundaries along with the number.

levels.1:
You ask a question and wait several seconds before anything appears. Once the answer starts, it pours out. Another service starts answering almost at once and then trickles along. Both get described as “the model is slow”, and the two symptoms usually have different causes.

Inference engines split the work into prefill and decode. Prefill processes text that is already known, which is your prompt. Decode extends the sequence by generating new tokens.

Every prompt token is available before the model starts answering. A well-organized engine can therefore process many prompt positions together, as long as no position reads ahead of itself. This pass builds the attention state that generation will reuse.

The answer tokens do not exist yet. The engine chooses one, feeds it back in to continue the calculation and repeats. That dependency makes decode behave very differently from prefill.

Time to first token (TTFT) is how long the first generated token takes to arrive, measured between whichever start and end points you choose. A high TTFT can come from waiting in a queue, preparing the input, processing the prompt or delivering the result.

Inter-token latency, also called time between tokens, is the gap between successive generated tokens. It describes how smoothly the answer flows once it has begun.

Throughput is the total work completed per second across all requests. A server answering a hundred people can post high throughput while each of them watches a slow answer, so always check whether a number describes one user or the whole system.

If a long document produces a long initial pause and then fast streaming, start with prompt processing and everything before it. If the first token is quick and the rest are slow, look at generation. Queueing and network delays can produce either symptom, so treat these as starting points.

When you evaluate an engine for your own fine-tuned model, record both the initial wait and the streaming speed. A single tokens-per-second figure leaves out half of what the user experiences.
levels.2:
The two phases cost different resources. Prefill over n prompt tokens multiplies every weight by n token vectors, so each byte of weight fetched supports about n multiply-adds, and attention adds work that grows with n times the visible length. Decode runs one new position per request. Each weight byte fetched supports only as many multiply-adds as there are requests in the batch, and every request’s cache must be read again. A long prompt therefore tends to keep the arithmetic units busy, while a small decode batch mostly waits on memory. The next lesson makes that precise.

Throughput and per-user speed use different denominators. If 64 requests each receive 30 tokens per second, each user sees 30 tokens per second and the system produces 64 × 30 = 1,920 tokens per second. Growing the batch usually raises the second number and lowers the first, because each step does more work and takes longer.

A useful decomposition is TTFT ≈ queue + preprocessing + prefill + first sample + delivery. Time per output token, TPOT, averages the later gaps: (end-to-end time − TTFT) / (output tokens − 1). Inter-token latency, ITL, is the distribution of the individual gaps. Their means match. Their tails do not, and the tails are what a user notices as stutter.

DeepInfer’s scheduler shows how an engine trades these off. In a NORMAL engine, each step is entirely a prompt step or entirely a decode step; SchedulerOutputs.prompt_run records which. In csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp, decode runs by default. Every 70 decode steps (DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL) the data-parallel ranks vote, and a prefill step happens only if every rank has a waiting prompt. Every 100 steps (DEEPINFER_PREFILL_ANY_ATTEMPT_INTERVAL) one rank with work is enough. A rank also declines to prefill while its KV cache is more than 90% full. The intervals exist because all ranks must run the same kind of step together.

Put invented numbers on it. If a decode step takes 25 ms, a prompt that arrives just after a prefill step can wait up to 70 steps, 1.75 s, before its prefill begins, or up to 2.5 s if no other rank has work. That wait is part of TTFT, and a timer around the model’s forward pass will never see it. When the prefill step does run, every in-flight answer pauses for its duration, so its users see one long gap. These are the costs of keeping prefill and decode on one engine. DeepSeek’s production deployment, by its Q&A, avoids them by running separate prefill and decode engines, the PROMPT and COMPLETION engine types.

Each prefill step has a token budget, max_num_batched_tokens (32,768 in the offline example). Chunked prefill splits a long prompt across several steps to fit the budget. It is off by default in EngineArgs, and without it a prompt longer than the budget is rejected. The Q&A describes a finer production rule: each prefill step gets a time budget, and a fitted quadratic cost model in the number of new tokens and the already-cached prefix length sets the largest chunk that fits.

Two more mechanisms change what the gaps look like. With asynchronous scheduling, which is on by default, the CPU schedules step N+1 and post-processes step N−1 while the GPU runs step N, so the GPU is not idle during bookkeeping. With speculative decoding, a decode step can emit several tokens per request. The Q&A reports about 3.2 accepted tokens per step at its operating point. A 30 ms step then averages about 9 ms per token, but tokens arrive in bursts, and an ITL histogram shows it.
levels.3:
The scheduling question was framed by a sequence of systems papers. Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues’ Orca (OSDI 2022) showed that admitting and retiring requests at every iteration, instead of once per batch, removes the wait for the slowest request in a batch. That made prefill and decode compete within the same steps. Amey Agrawal and colleagues’ Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024) named the resulting “generation stalls”, where a long prefill pauses every running answer, and proposed stall-free batching: split prompts into chunks and add a chunk to each decode step, trading a slightly longer TTFT for steady gaps. Yinmin Zhong and colleagues’ DistServe and Pratyush Patel and colleagues’ Splitwise (both 2024) argued instead for putting the phases on different machines, each sized and parallelized for its own bottleneck, at the cost of moving the KV cache between them.

DistServe also sharpened the metric. It defines goodput as the highest request rate at which a target fraction of requests, for example 90%, meet both a TTFT objective and a per-token objective. That is the right shape for a product decision. A configuration with higher peak throughput can have lower goodput if it misses the latency targets more often. Comparing systems at matched objectives, rather than at their own best points, is the main methodological advance of this line of work.

DeepInfer sits at a definite point in this space. Its colocated NORMAL engine alternates whole prefill and decode steps, timed by rank-wide votes, rather than mixing chunks into decode steps as Sarathi-Serve does. That keeps every step uniform across data-parallel ranks and is easier to make batch-invariant, at the price of stalls and queueing in a colocated deployment. Production avoids that price through disaggregation, which the Q&A reports at roughly one prefill GPU per decode GPU. The release ships the engine types for that split but not the load balancers that make it work, so an outside team running a single offline engine is measuring a different system from the one DeepSeek describes.

Tail latency needs its own reasoning. Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso’s “The Tail at Scale” (2013) showed that in systems with many components, rare slow events dominate what users see. Queueing makes tails explode near capacity. In the textbook single-server queue with random arrivals, mean time in the system is 1 / (μ − λ) for service rate μ and arrival rate λ. At 100 requests per second of capacity, 80 arriving gives 50 ms and 95 arriving gives 200 ms. The server is barely busier, and the wait has quadrupled. A benchmark that sends all requests at time zero has no arrivals at all, so it cannot show this.

Load generators can hide the effect too. A closed-loop client that waits for each response before sending the next slows down exactly when the server does. Gil Tene called the resulting bias “coordinated omission”: the slowest periods are sampled least. Open-loop generators send on a schedule regardless of responses, and replaying real arrival traces, such as the Azure traces the Splitwise authors released, adds the burstiness that Poisson arrivals leave out.

Optimizations interact with load in ways that only measurement reveals. DeepSeek’s Q&A reports that confidence-scheduled speculative verification, compared with always verifying five draft tokens, changes estimated throughput per rank by −1.5% at 16 concurrent sequences, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. The same mechanism hurts at light load and helps at heavy load, because it saves verification work that only matters once the GPU is saturated. These figures are estimates derived from the authors’ own benchmark data. Open problems include scheduling with real arrival processes and long shared prefixes, predicting prefill cost well enough to set chunk budgets, and defining goodput for agent workloads where one task spans dozens of requests.

LESSONS.title: Why GPUs wait: memory, math and kernels
LESSONS.goal: Explain why an expensive GPU can wait for data instead of doing useful arithmetic.
LESSONS.recall: How do capacity and bandwidth differ?
LESSONS.predict: If weights take 8 ms to read but arithmetic takes 1 ms, will twice the arithmetic speed halve the step?
example: A toy operation reads 8 GB at 1,000 GB per second, and its arithmetic takes 1 millisecond. What is the main limit?
Start with the transfer: 8 GB divided by 1,000 GB per second is 0.008 seconds, or 8 milliseconds. Keeping bytes and bytes per second in matching units makes the answer come out as a time.
Set that beside the 1 millisecond of arithmetic. Even if the two overlap perfectly, the operation takes at least the larger time, 8 milliseconds. Less overlap or extra overhead makes it longer.

Doubling the arithmetic speed turns 1 millisecond into half a millisecond and leaves the 8-millisecond transfer in place. Under these assumptions, cutting data traffic or reusing the fetched data for more work is the more promising direction.

questions.prompt: When do faster math units help least?
options: Memory movement dominates
Arithmetic dominates
The model has a name
questions.why: Speeding up a resource that is not the limit leaves the limiting cost in place. In the 8 ms versus 1 ms example, even infinitely fast arithmetic could save at most that 1 ms.
questions.hint: Compare the two time estimates.
option_feedback: Correct: when moving data takes longer than the arithmetic, faster arithmetic shortens a cost that was not setting the pace.
When arithmetic dominates, faster math units attack exactly the limiting cost, so this is where they help most.
A model’s name has no effect on execution. The answer depends on which resource is the limit.

questions.prompt: A decode step must read 8 GB of weights at 1 TB per second. What is the shortest that step can take from memory traffic alone?
options: 8 seconds
8 milliseconds
8 microseconds
questions.why: With decimal units, 1 TB/s is 1,000 GB/s, so reading 8 GB takes at least 8 / 1,000 = 0.008 seconds. Below the ridge point, adding tokens to the batch does not shorten that floor.
questions.hint: A TB is 1,000 GB here.
option_feedback: 8 seconds would need a rate of 1 GB per second, a thousand times slower.
Correct: 1 TB is 1,000 GB, so 8 / 1,000 seconds is 8 milliseconds.
8 microseconds would need a rate of 1,000 TB per second, a thousand times faster.

questions.prompt: Why can fusion help without reducing mathematical FLOPs?
options: It changes all probabilities to zero
It can remove intermediate writes and launch overhead
It trains a smaller model automatically
questions.why: Execution cost includes moving intermediate results through memory and dispatching each kernel. Fusion reduces both while doing the same arithmetic.
questions.hint: Math count is only one budget.
option_feedback: Fusion leaves the mathematical result unchanged. Setting probabilities to zero would change the model’s output.
Correct: a fused kernel keeps intermediates in fast memory and launches once, cutting traffic and dispatch cost.
Fusion is an execution change applied to the existing model. It does no training.

transfer: A teammate suggests using a smaller numerical format to speed up your endpoint. What would you want to know before adopting it?
Identifies limiting operation and resource
Checks hardware/kernel support
Tests numerical/task quality and end-to-end latency

I would first find which operation and which resource are taking the time. Storing fewer bytes helps when data movement is the limit, and it does nothing for a scheduling delay or a slow conversion step. I would check that the hardware and kernels support the format, compare outputs with a reference and evaluate task quality. Then I would rerun the same workload to see whether the latency users see actually improves.
LESSONS.takeaway: Execution time can be limited by moving data, doing arithmetic, or coordinating the work.

activity.title: Choose which limit to investigate first.
activity.intro: For one toy operation, the amount of arithmetic divided by the arithmetic rate gives 2 milliseconds. Moving the needed data at the available bandwidth gives 8 milliseconds. Assume ideal overlap between the two. This is an estimate for one operation, not a measured whole-model latency.

fields.label: What is the ideal lower bound in milliseconds?
fields.why: With ideal overlap, the lower bound is the larger cost: max(2, 8) = 8 milliseconds.

fields.label: Which limit dominates this estimate?
options: compute
The arithmetic rate
memory
The rate at which data can move
fields.why: The data movement takes longer than the arithmetic under these assumptions. Faster arithmetic alone would leave the 8-millisecond limit.

fields.label: Which observation would best test whether that estimate describes a real run?
options: peak
Only the advertised peak arithmetic rate
trace
A runtime trace showing where time and data movement go
name
The name of the model
fields.why: A trace can expose actual waiting, transfers, and execution. The toy estimate is a hypothesis about the limiting resource, not evidence that a real run reaches that limit.

activity.conclusion: A simple estimate tells you what to ask the profiler. The observed execution should decide which change you try.

levels.1:
A GPU is a processor built to perform many numerical operations in parallel. Language models are mostly arithmetic, so GPUs suit them well. Its arithmetic units still cannot work on numbers that have not reached them yet.

Model weights and working state live in memory. During execution the data has to travel from that memory to the units doing the calculation, and some results have to travel back. That movement takes time.

Memory capacity is how much data fits. Memory bandwidth is how many bytes can move per second. A model can fit comfortably in memory and still run slowly because every step has to move a lot of data.

You will often see HBM, short for high-bandwidth memory, which is the GPU’s large main memory. Smaller and much faster storage sits closer to the arithmetic units. Much of an engine developer’s work goes into arranging calculations so the data they need is already close by.

Picture an operation that needs eight milliseconds to fetch its data and only one millisecond to do its arithmetic. Doubling the arithmetic speed leaves the eight-millisecond transfer exactly where it was. Data movement sets this operation’s pace.

Now group enough work together that the same fetched weights get used many times. Each byte moved then supports more arithmetic, and the arithmetic units stay busier until some other cost becomes the limit.

Underneath, an engine runs kernels, the programs that carry out individual GPU operations. A better kernel might avoid writing an intermediate result out to slow memory, lay data out more efficiently, or merge several small operations into one.

Storing each number in fewer bytes can also help. That is one purpose of quantization, which represents values in a more limited format. It brings its own questions about rounding, model quality and whether the hardware has an efficient implementation.

So when someone says an optimization makes inference faster, ask which cost it removes, and then check whether that cost dominates your workload. Saving memory capacity and cutting execution time are related, and they are measured differently.
levels.2:
Make the bound concrete with one matrix product. A batch X[B,d] multiplied by a BF16 weight mapping d to h costs 2Bdh FLOPs and moves about 2(dh + Bd + Bh) bytes: the weight once, the inputs and the outputs. When B is much smaller than d and h, the weight term dominates and arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte, is about 2Bdh / 2dh = B. A device’s ridge point is its compute rate divided by its bandwidth. NVIDIA’s H100 SXM datasheet lists 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute and 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, a ridge near 295 FLOPs per byte. Below roughly 295 tokens per step, this product is limited by memory on that device.

This explains decode economics. If a step must read 8 GB of weights at 3.35 TB/s, it cannot finish in less than 2.4 ms, whether the batch holds one token or two hundred. Within that range, larger batches are almost free per token. Storing weights in FP8 halves the bytes, and the FP8 compute rate is double the BF16 rate, so the ridge measured in tokens stays about the same. Mixture-of-experts models complicate the count, because each expert sees only the tokens routed to it. DeepSeek’s Q&A gives this as a reason to spread decode across 64–128 GPUs: wide expert parallelism raises each expert’s batch and cuts memory traffic per step. DeepInfer targets NVIDIA SM100 (Blackwell) and Huawei Ascend parts, whose numbers differ, but the reasoning is the same.

Inside a GPU, data moves through a hierarchy: HBM, then a shared L2 cache, then each streaming multiprocessor’s shared memory and registers, each level smaller and faster than the last. A matrix kernel loads tiles of both operands into shared memory, reuses each tile many times from there and writes only the finished output. DeepInfer’s dense products go through DeepGEMM (bf16_gemm_nt and FP8 variants in layers/linear.py). Its FP8 path quantizes activations to E4M3 with one power-of-two scale per 32 channels (get_fp8_cast_params), a format the tensor cores consume directly.

Fusion attacks the traffic between kernels. Run separately, normalization, rotary embedding, a rotation, an FP8 cast and a cache store would each read their input from HBM and write their output back. DeepInfer’s fused_norm_rope_hadamard_cast_store_kvcache in tilelang_ops/fused_transform.py does all five in one kernel, so the intermediates stay on chip. The FLOP count is unchanged. What disappears is four round trips through HBM and four kernel launches.

Launch overhead matters most in decode, where each kernel does little work. The CPU spends microseconds enqueueing each launch, and a step can contain hundreds. CUDA graphs record the whole sequence once and replay it with one call. DeepInfer captures graphs for fixed batch sizes in deepinfer/worker/cuda_graph_runner.py: build_graph_batch_sizes produces 1, 2 and 4, then every multiple of 8 up to the maximum, and select picks the smallest captured size that fits. Nine tokens run as a 16-row graph, so 7 of the 16 rows (44%) are padding. Fifty-seven tokens run as 64, and 11% is padding. Finer intervals waste less compute and cost more graph memory and capture time.

The engine also guards the CPU side. execute_main_model in worker/model_runner.py runs inside forbid_cuda_sync(), which raises an error on any blocking CPU–GPU synchronization during launch. A single stray .item() in a forward pass would stall the CPU until the GPU drained, and the asynchronous scheduler that overlaps CPU bookkeeping with GPU work would stop overlapping. tests/test_cuda_sync_guards.py enforces the rule.

Quantization buys bytes at a price in precision, and the format determines that price. Block scaling with 32 elements per scale limits how far one outlier can distort its neighbors. DeepSeek’s Q&A lists MXFP4 (FP4 values with one power-of-two scale per 32) for routed expert weights and an FP4 format with E4M3 scales per 16 values for the main KV cache. A narrower format helps only where bytes were the limit, and only if a kernel consumes it without a separate pass to expand it back to BF16.
levels.3:
Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson introduced the roofline model in 2009 as a visual bound for any kernel on any machine: performance cannot exceed the compute peak, or bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, whichever is lower. Reiner Pope and colleagues at Google applied this reasoning to transformer inference in 2022. They showed how batch size, sequence length and partitioning across chips move each operation between the two limits, and how latency and cost trade against each other. The Scaling Book’s roofline and inference chapters, written by Google DeepMind researchers, are the most direct modern treatment. All of them give bounds. The gap between a bound and a measured kernel is where the engineering happens.

The usual summary statistic is model FLOPs utilization, MFU, introduced in Aakanksha Chowdhery and colleagues’ 2022 PaLM paper: the model’s necessary FLOPs per second divided by the hardware peak. It needs accounting decisions. DeepInfer’s csrc/engine/flops_estimator.hpp weights each contraction by precision (FP4 as 1, FP8 as 2, BF16 as 4) to express work in FP8-equivalent FLOPs. It excludes the draft model’s work, padding and replicated experts, and omits normalizations. Each choice is defensible, and each changes the number. Two MFU figures are comparable only under the same conventions.

The case for attacking data movement was made empirically. Andrei Ivanov, Nikoli Dryden, Tal Ben-Nun, Shigang Li and Torsten Hoefler’s “Data Movement Is All You Need” (MLSys 2021) profiled BERT training and found that matrix multiplications accounted for nearly all the FLOPs but a much smaller share of the runtime. The rest went to memory-bound element-wise operations and normalizations, which fusion and better layouts recovered. Tri Dao, Daniel Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra and Christopher Ré’s FlashAttention (2022) turned the argument into an analysis of memory traffic.
