Using Maxim Milakov and Natalia Gimelshein’s online softmax, it tiled exact attention so the full score matrix never reached HBM. FlashAttention-2 improved work partitioning, and FlashAttention-3 (Jay Shah and colleagues, 2024) used Hopper’s asynchronous copy engines and FP8. DeepSeek’s FlashMLA, which DeepInfer calls, specializes the idea for latent attention.

Kernel gains are not end-to-end gains, and DeepSeek’s Q&A gives a clean example. It says the public FlashMLA lacks one hand-tuned assembly optimization that makes the internal decode kernel 5–10% faster, yet end-to-end performance differs by at most 5%. Attention is one kernel among many in a step. The same logic limits every microbenchmark. Reported speedups need the share of step time the kernel occupies, measured on the target batch size and context length. Kan Zhu and colleagues’ NanoFlow (2024) went the other way, splitting a batch into nano-batches so that compute-bound, memory-bound and network-bound operations overlap on one device, which raises utilization without making any one kernel faster.

Quantization evidence is model-specific. Tim Dettmers and colleagues’ LLM.int8() (2022) found outlier features of large magnitude emerging in models around 6.7 billion parameters, which broke naive 8-bit schemes. Guangxuan Xiao and colleagues’ SmoothQuant moved activation outliers into the weights. Elias Frantar and colleagues’ GPTQ and Ji Lin and colleagues’ AWQ reached 3–4-bit weights with small perplexity loss on the models they tested. Paulius Micikevicius and colleagues defined the FP8 formats in 2022, and Bita Darvish Rouhani and colleagues’ microscaling (MX) formats standardized block-scaled FP8, FP6 and FP4 with a shared power-of-two scale per 32 elements. Perplexity on generic text often misses damage that shows up on reasoning or long-context tasks. DeepInfer ships task evaluations (eval/ covers AIME, GPQA and HLE) as well as a perplexity reference in tests/models/offline_decode_ppl.json.

How kernels get written is itself contested. Philippe Tillet, H. T. Kung and David Cox’s Triton (2019) made block-level GPU programming accessible from Python. Benjamin Spector and colleagues’ ThunderKittens (2024) built kernels from small tile primitives, and TileLang, which DeepInfer uses for its custom operators, takes a similar tile-level approach. At the far end, “megakernels” fuse an entire forward pass into one persistent kernel to remove launch gaps altogether. The Q&A says DeepSeek’s Mega MoE fused kernel beats unfused MoE at every expert-parallel and batch size within a scale-up domain. Open problems include keeping kernels portable across vendors (DeepInfer maintains separate NVIDIA and Ascend paths), predicting real performance from a roofline when communication and scheduling interleave, and validating aggressive low-precision formats on the tasks users actually run.

LESSONS.title: Batching and overlapping CPU with GPU work
LESSONS.goal: Explain how serving requests together saves work, and why it can still make someone wait.
LESSONS.recall: Why can reusing the same weights across requests improve arithmetic intensity?
LESSONS.predict: If one request finishes early in a fixed batch, must its slot stay empty?
example: A batch holds a short answer and a long answer. The short one finishes first. What should the engine do with its place?
The finished request needs no more model steps. Its state can be released once nothing still reads it, while the long answer keeps its own separate state.
A fixed batch leaves the short request’s place empty until the whole group finishes. Continuous batching admits a waiting request between steps and gives it fresh state of its own.

Reusing the place raises overall throughput. The newcomer still waited before it was admitted, though, and every step still takes time. Measure those delays before claiming that each user got a faster answer.

questions.prompt: Continuous batching lets the engine…
options: Share one request’s private history with everyone
Replace completed requests between steps
Skip attention for every request
questions.why: The active group is re-formed between steps, so a waiting request can take the place of one that finished.
questions.hint: Which unit finishes independently?
option_feedback: Batched requests share weights and execution steps, and each keeps its own private history.
Right. The group changes between steps, so a waiting request can fill a finished request’s place.
Every request still needs attention over its own context; batching only groups the work.

questions.prompt: A decode step spends 2 ms scheduling on the CPU, 8 ms executing on the GPU and 1 ms post-processing on the CPU. With the CPU work fully overlapped with GPU work, what is the steady-state time per step?
options: 11 ms, because overlap leaves every phase in place
8 ms, because the 3 ms of CPU work hides under the GPU work
3 ms, because only the CPU work remains on the critical path
questions.why: In steady state the CPU prepares step N+1 and finishes step N−1 while the GPU runs step N, so the longer lane, 8 ms of GPU work, sets the pace.
questions.hint: Which lane is longer once both run at the same time?
option_feedback: 11 ms is the serial time. Overlap removes the GPU's idle gap while the CPU works.
Right. The 3 ms of CPU work fits inside the 8 ms of GPU work, so the step takes 8 ms.
The GPU still needs 8 ms per step; overlap cannot make the device work disappear.

questions.prompt: An async rewrite returns each step's output objects to their pool immediately, deleting the deferred release. What is the main risk?
options: Slightly more code to review
A later step reuses memory that a consumer of the earlier step is still reading
Lower GPU utilization during prefill
questions.why: Under overlap, step N's outputs are still being read while step N+1 runs. Recycling them early lets new data overwrite bytes that still have a reader.
questions.hint: Who still holds a reference to those objects when the next step starts?
option_feedback: The risk is a real lifetime bug that a style review would not catch.
Right. The deferred release exists so that nothing is recycled until every reader has finished.
Utilization is not the concern; correctness of shared buffers is.

transfer: Explain one useful way for CPU work and GPU work to overlap, and one moment when the engine must still wait.
Shows two execution resources
Names the data dependency causing a wait
Includes startup or draining cost

The CPU can prepare independent metadata for a future step while the GPU calculates the current step, so the GPU does not sit idle afterward. The CPU must still wait before it reads results that have not finished, and it cannot release or overwrite buffers that an unfinished operation still uses. Overlap also has a startup cost before the pipeline fills and a draining cost at the end.
LESSONS.takeaway: Batching spreads execution costs across requests, and the scheduler decides whose work gets those savings and when.

levels.1:
Suppose ten people are using the same model at once. Their questions and conversation histories differ, but every one of them runs through the same weights. An engine can take advantage of that by organizing some of their calculations together instead of running each request from start to finish on its own.

Grouping work this way is called batching. Each weight read from memory now serves several positions, and many small matrix operations merge into a few large ones that keep the GPU’s arithmetic units busy. Fixed costs, such as launching each GPU operation, are spread over more useful work.

The requests still have separate lives. One person asks for a one-line answer; another asks for a long report. If the engine fixes the group at the start and keeps it unchanged until everyone finishes, the short request’s place sits idle while the long one keeps generating.

Continuous batching lets the active group change between execution steps. When a request finishes, a waiting request takes its place on the next step, with its own state. The hardware stays busier, and no request ever has to share another’s conversation.

Deciding what runs in each step is the job of the engine’s scheduler. It has to stay inside memory limits while dividing each step among new prompts, long prompts and answers that are already streaming back to users.

The CPU can also leave the GPU idle. The CPU runs most of the engine’s coordination code: it prepares each step, launches the GPU operations and processes their results. If the GPU finishes a step and then waits while the CPU prepares the next one, arithmetic capacity goes unused.

Some of that preparation can overlap with device work. While the GPU runs one step, the CPU can prepare the parts of a later step that do not depend on results still being computed. Engines call this asynchronous execution. The 2024 NanoFlow paper carries the same idea further, overlapping compute, memory and network work so that no single resource sits waiting on another.

None of this guarantees that a particular request gets faster. A larger batch takes longer per step, and a new request may wait for a free place. Total tokens per second can rise while one user waits longer for the first word of their answer.

A scheduler is making a tradeoff under real demand. To judge one, measure both the useful work completed per second and the waits that individual requests experience.
levels.2:
Start with one decode step for a batch of B requests. Each request contributes one new position (more under speculative decoding), and the step must read every active weight from GPU memory once. For a model whose active weights take W bytes, the weight read alone costs about W divided by memory bandwidth, whatever B is. With invented numbers, 30 GB of active weights on a GPU with 3 TB/s of bandwidth is a 10 ms floor per step. At B = 1 that 10 ms buys one token; at B = 64 the same read buys 64. The arithmetic grows with B, and so does the attention work, which reads each request's own KV cache. Eventually arithmetic or KV reads catch up with the weight read, and from then on each extra request makes the step longer.

DeepInfer's scheduler lives in C++, in csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp, and LLMEngine.step calls it once per step. It keeps a waiting queue of prompts, a prompted queue of requests whose prefill is done, and a running list. Two budgets bound every step: max_num_seqs caps how many requests take part, and max_num_batched_tokens caps how many positions the step computes. In _schedule_prefill, a prompt that does not fit in the remaining token budget is cut into a chunk (chunked prefill), and _adjust_chunk_size moves the cut so it never falls inside an image's tokens. In _schedule_decode, every running request needs room for its next position. When the block manager has no free block, the scheduler preempts a running request. Depending on stop_preempted_request, that request either ends with FINISHED_PREEMPTED or is reset and pushed back to the front of waiting to be recomputed. Requests with structured output always stop, because their grammar state cannot be recomputed.

A step in the default engine is either all prefill or all decode, and every data-parallel rank must agree, because all of them join the same expert-parallel communication inside the step. _schedule settles this with a vote, an all-reduce across the group. A rank with nothing to do runs an empty placeholder step so the collectives still line up.

Now the CPU side. DeepSeek's deployment Q&A splits decode step N into schedule(N) → forward(N) → sample(N) → post-process(N). Scheduling and post-processing are pure CPU work, and post-processing must wait for the sampled tokens. Run serially, the GPU idles during post-process(N) and schedule(N+1). With 2 ms of scheduling, 8 ms of GPU work and 1 ms of post-processing, each step takes 11 ms. If the 3 ms of CPU work runs while the GPU computes, the steady-state step drops to 8 ms. That is 27% less time per step, or about 37% more steps per second. The first step still pays its setup and the last still drains. If CPU work grew past 8 ms, the CPU would set the pace instead. llm_engine.py carries a TODO to remove O(number of requests) Python work from each decode step for this reason.

The overlap is built in Worker.execute_model_step (deepinfer/worker/worker.py). It runs four stages in order: forward the current step, post-process the previous step, sample the current step, and, for decode steps under DEEPINFER_ZERO_OVERHEAD_SCHEDULING, store the current step's state in prev_step_state so that its post-processing overlaps the next forward. Prefill steps are post-processed straight away.

The cost of the overlap is that the CPU schedules step N+1 before it knows what step N produced. It does not yet know how many draft tokens were accepted, so it does not know each sequence's true length. _correct_seqlens_qk handles this. It builds a remap from each request in the new batch to its row in the previous batch (−1 for newcomers) and corrects the lengths on the GPU from the previous step's num_accepted_tokens, so the CPU never has to wait. Lifetimes get the same care. step's docstring warns that returned outputs are released on the next call unless cloned, and the DeferredRelease class holds a step's metadata and outputs until the next pre_sampler_sync, so nothing is recycled while a consumer may still be reading it.
levels.3:
Continuous batching has a short, traceable history. Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues' Orca (OSDI 2022) introduced iteration-level scheduling: the batch is re-formed at every model step, and attention, whose shape differs per request, is run separately while the other operations are batched (they called this selective batching). vLLM added paged KV memory, so a request could join a batch without a large reservation in advance. Since then, research has mostly asked how to share a step between prefill, which is heavy on arithmetic, and decode, which is light on arithmetic and sensitive to latency.

Two answers compete. Amey Agrawal and colleagues' Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024) cuts prompts into chunks and mixes them into decode steps, so a long prompt never stalls the streams already running. Their term is stall-free batching. DistServe (Yinmin Zhong and colleagues, OSDI 2024) and Splitwise (Pratyush Patel and colleagues, ISCA 2024) move prefill and decode onto different machines, so the two phases stop interfering and each pool can be sized and parallelized for its own phase. DistServe also popularized goodput: requests per second served within their latency targets. DeepSeek's production system takes the second route. Its Q&A describes separate vision-encoder, prefill and decode deployments. A prefill step's chunk size comes from solving a fitted quadratic cost model cost(q, c), where q is the new tokens and c the prefix already computed, against a per-step time budget in nanoseconds and a 32,768-token cap. The released DeepInfer engine, by contrast, alternates whole prefill and decode steps when one engine does both.

For overlap, the Q&A names SGLang and NanoFlow as prior art. NanoFlow (Kan Zhu, Baris Kasikci and colleagues, 2024) goes further than hiding CPU work: it splits a batch into nano-batches inside one GPU so that compute-bound, memory-bound and network-bound operations run at the same time. The paper argues that serving is usually compute-bound, reports up to 1.91× throughput over the systems it compared against, and puts NanoFlow at 50–72% of its own estimate of optimal throughput. Those are the authors' measurements on their models and workloads.

Judge scheduling claims by the curve, not by a single point. DeepInfer's README plots decode output throughput against per-user speed, measured on 64 SM100 GPUs. A scheduler change is an improvement only if it moves that frontier, giving more throughput at the same per-user speed, or more speed at the same throughput. A single tokens-per-second number can come from simply running a larger batch. Report time to first token and inter-token latency percentiles at the concurrency you intend to serve, and say how many requests were sampled.

Overlap also creates its own bugs: data that is still in use gets released or overwritten. In DeepInfer, DeferredRelease waits a full step before returning metadata and output objects to their pools. Unpinning cloned KV blocks also waits on a CUDA event that marks the end of the copy. A copy or deferred free that looks wasteful may be what keeps a later step from overwriting bytes that an earlier consumer is still reading. Before deleting one, find every reader of that buffer and the event that orders it. Test early stops, cancellations, preemption with recompute and mixed sequence lengths, because each of these changes which request occupies a row between the step that was scheduled and the step that is post-processed.

Several problems remain open. Output lengths are unknown at admission, so a preemption policy is a bet, and recomputing a preempted request repeats its prefill. Speculative decoding interacts with asynchronous scheduling: in DeepInfer the CPU fixes only the total verification budget for step N+1, because step N's confidence estimates have not returned, and a GPU kernel assigns the per-request lengths. And the CPU's work per step grows with the number of active requests, so at very large batches the coordinator, rather than the GPU, can become the bottleneck.

LESSONS.title: KV memory, paging and prefix reuse
LESSONS.goal: Distinguish keeping a request’s state, organizing its memory and reusing another request’s prefix.
LESSONS.recall: What computation does a KV cache avoid, and what work remains?
LESSONS.predict: If two prompts share the same first 1,000 tokens, can that prefix be reused when their model weights differ?
example: Two requests use the same prompt IDs. The second uses a different adapter that changes attention. Can it reuse the first request’s KV?
The first request’s keys and values came out of its base weights and its adapter. They are numerical results of that particular computation, and the prompt IDs alone do not determine them.

The second adapter can produce different attention state from the same IDs. Reusing the first request’s state would silently mix values from two different models, and the equal tensor shapes would hide the mistake.

Put the model and adapter identity into the cache key, or invalidate the affected state when the adapter changes. To check the fix, alternate the two adapters and compare cached results against uncached reference runs.

questions.prompt: Paging and prefix caching are…
options: The same mechanism
Allocation management versus reuse of computed prefixes
Both just text compression
questions.why: They can be combined, but they remove different kinds of waste: fragmented memory and repeated prefill.
questions.hint: One asks where state fits; the other asks whether it already exists.
option_feedback: They often work together, yet one decides where state lives and the other decides whether it already exists.
Right. Paging manages where blocks go; prefix caching skips recomputing a beginning that was already processed.
Neither one compresses text. Both handle numerical attention state.

questions.prompt: A model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and stores BF16 (2-byte) values in a conventional cache. How many bytes does each token add?
options: 64 KiB
128 KiB
512 KiB
questions.why: 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB.
questions.hint: Count keys and values separately.
option_feedback: 64 KiB counts only keys or only values; the cache holds both.
Right. 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes is 128 KiB per token.
512 KiB would need 32 KV heads; grouped-query attention shares 8 among the query heads.

questions.prompt: A team wants to key the prefix cache on token IDs alone, arguing that two LoRA adapters of the same rank produce tensors of the same shape. Your verdict?
options: Accept: equal shapes mean the cached values are interchangeable
Reject: the adapter is an input to the cached keys and values, so it belongs in the key
Accept if hit rate rises after the change
questions.why: Keys and values are numerical results of the weights that computed them. Equal shapes hide the mismatch rather than ruling it out.
questions.hint: List every input that determined the cached numbers.
option_feedback: Shape says nothing about values; two adapters can compute different keys for the same IDs.
Right. Include model and adapter identity, then test by alternating adapters against uncached references.
A higher hit rate would be the symptom of the bug: wrong state found more often.

transfer: A cache finds more matching prefixes, but requests take longer. Give a possible explanation and a measurement that would test it.
Includes transfer or lookup cost
Compares saved computation with added cost
Measures latency, not hit rate alone

Looking up or fetching the saved state may take longer than processing the prefix again. A hit shows that stored work was found; it says nothing about whether fetching it saved time. I would time lookup, transfer and the remaining prompt computation separately for hits and misses, then compare time to first token on a representative workload. I would also check whether the transfers slow down other requests.
LESSONS.takeaway: A cache helps only when it saves the right computation, under a compatible model, and returns it faster than recomputing would.

levels.1:
You have already met the KV cache, the keys and values saved from earlier positions of a request. As the answer grows, so does that saved state. Keeping it spares the engine from recomputing earlier keys and values at every generation step.

Serving many requests at once raises two further questions. How should the engine allocate space for sequences that keep growing? And can a new request reuse work that an earlier request already did?

Start with allocation. If every request needed one large, continuous stretch of memory, requests that grow and finish at different times would leave awkward gaps between them. The engine can instead cut the state into fixed-size blocks and keep a table that maps each request’s logical positions to the blocks it owns.

This is paging, the idea at the center of the 2023 PagedAttention paper that introduced vLLM. It works much like an operating system mapping a program’s virtual pages onto scattered physical memory. Blocks are handed out as a sequence grows, and requests with identical beginnings can point at the same blocks.

Now the repeated work. Suppose thousands of requests begin with the same long system instructions. The engine can keep the saved state for that common beginning and attach it to each new request instead of processing it again. This is prefix caching; a prefix is simply the shared beginning of a sequence. The SGLang paper organizes these saved prefixes in a tree, a design it calls RadixAttention.

The match has to be exact in a specific sense. The text must tokenize to the same IDs, and the model that processes those IDs must perform the same computation. Swap in a different adapter and the keys and values change, even though the prompt text is identical.

A saved prefix also has to be worth fetching. It might live on another machine, and looking it up, transferring it and attaching it to the new request all take time. If recomputing the prefix would have been quicker, a cache hit makes the user wait longer.

Hit rate therefore tells only part of the story. It counts how often stored work was found and says nothing about whether retrieving it made the service faster.

Memory grows with the amount of live context. More requests and longer histories mean more retained attention state. In a conventional cache, doubling both the number of requests and their context lengths makes the raw state four times larger. The exact storage formula depends on the model’s attention design, and compressed designs do not use the conventional layout.
levels.2:
For a conventional cache, count bytes per token first. Each layer stores one key and one value vector per KV head, so bytes_per_token = 2 × layers × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element, and the total multiplies that by the number of live tokens across all requests. Take a model shaped like Llama 3 8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, BF16 values of 2 bytes. That gives 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB per token. Thirty-two requests of 8,192 tokens each hold 262,144 tokens, which comes to 32 GiB of cache before any working memory. With 32 KV heads and no grouped-query attention, the same model would need 512 KiB per token, four times as much.

DeepSeek V4.1 does not fit this formula, and deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py shows why. The main cache, ca_cache, has shape [num_blocks, block_size // ratio, 1, bytes_per_token]. Positions are compressed by a ratio before storage. Each stored entry is a latent vector of 288 bytes in a per-16 FP4 format or 528 bytes in MXFP8 (512 bytes of FP8 data plus 16 bytes of scales). A separate indexer cache, ica_cache, holds FP4 keys that sparse attention uses to choose which blocks to read. The sliding-window state is a third kind of memory. It does not live in pages at all: swa_cache is indexed by sequence, with one fixed slot per request of window + DEEPINFER_MAX_BACKTRACKING_TOKENS tokens. With a 128-token window and the default of 6 backtracking tokens (one more than the 5 draft tokens), that is 134 tokens per layer. The Q&A gives the persisted size as 20 layers × 134 tokens × 528 B = 1,415,040 bytes per sequence. Paged memory grows with context length; state slots grow with the number of concurrent requests (get_num_state_slots allocates 1.2 × max_num_seqs + 1).

The pages themselves are managed in csrc/engine/block_manager.hpp. Free blocks sit in a doubly linked list, and block 0 is reserved to mean "no block". Each block has a reference count. allocate pops a free block and sets its count to 1, pin_block adds a reference when another sequence shares the block, and free returns the block to the list only when the count reaches zero. can_allocate_nolock answers OK, LATER (wait for blocks to free up) or NEVER (the request needs more blocks than exist, so it is rejected).

Forking a request shows how sharing works. When fork_seq creates a branch from a computed prefix, the new sequence starts with the parent's block table. When the branch is scheduled, every full block stays shared. The partially filled last block is copied into a fresh block, because the branch will write new positions into it and must not overwrite the parent's. The scheduler records each (source, destination) pair in clone_blocks and clones the state slot as well. This is copy-on-write at block granularity, the same idea PagedAttention used for parallel sampling.

Whether a prefix hit pays off is a comparison of times. Under invented but plausible numbers: a 10,000-token prefix in the Llama-shaped model is about 1.25 GiB of KV. Fetching it over a 25 GB/s path takes roughly 54 ms. Recomputing it takes about 2 × 8×10⁹ parameters × 10⁴ tokens = 1.6×10¹⁴ floating-point operations, around 0.4 s at an effective 400 TFLOP/s. That hit is clearly worth it. For a 200-token prefix the recompute costs a few milliseconds, so a fixed lookup or network round trip of similar size erases the gain. DeepSeek's Q&A describes a three-stage hit path: a metadata-only hash-chain match before routing, which cannot be hidden; an asynchronous fetch from the storage cluster into host shared memory; and a swap-in to GPU memory that overlaps layer-by-layer with the forward pass. The swap-in uses GPUDirect RDMA, because the GPU's copy engine performed poorly on many small block copies.
levels.3:
Paging comes from Woosuk Kwon and colleagues' PagedAttention paper (SOSP 2023), which introduced vLLM. Systems before it reserved contiguous KV space for each request's maximum length. vLLM allocates blocks on demand and shares them by reference count, and the authors report 2–4× higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency. The gain grew with longer sequences, larger models and decoding methods that share prefixes, such as beam search and parallel sampling. Treat those figures as the authors' measurements on their workloads. The general lesson holds: when memory capacity limits batch size, reclaiming wasted memory turns directly into throughput.

Prefix reuse across requests took two directions. Lianmin Zheng, Ying Sheng and colleagues' SGLang stores prefixes in a radix tree (RadixAttention), evicts them least-recently-used first, and makes the scheduler cache-aware, preferring requests that share long cached prefixes. Other systems moved the cache off the GPU. CachedAttention (Bin Gao and colleagues, USENIX ATC 2024) keeps multi-turn conversation caches in host memory and on disk. Mooncake, from Moonshot AI, builds its whole serving architecture around a disaggregated KV store. DeepSeek's Q&A describes the same kind of design: block KV lives on a dedicated 3FS storage cluster with 10+2 erasure coding. Because any prefill machine can read any prefix, routing ignores prefix affinity. This deliberately gives up the cache-aware routing that SGLang relies on, so that load balancing stays simple. The Q&A reports TTLs of 3 days for agent traffic and 7 days for chatbot traffic. Chatbot traffic keeps the longer TTL because a few prefixes are read very many times; a 3-day TTL would cost it 0.5–1% of hit rate. Those numbers are author-reported, and the cache code itself is not in the open release.

Exact prefix matching is where the approach breaks. In retrieval-augmented generation the same document chunks recur in different orders, so they are not shared prefixes. CacheBlend (Jiayi Yao and colleagues, EuroSys 2025) reuses such non-prefix chunks and recomputes a small subset of tokens to repair the attention between them. That reuse is an approximation, with a quality cost that has to be measured. Exact reuse also needs every input that shaped the cached values to match: weights, adapter, tokenization, position encoding and storage format. DeepInfer adds a model-specific rule. The hit length is set by the block cache, but the last 128-token block is recomputed whenever its sliding-window state is missing, and no hit may exceed L − 134 tokens for an input of length L.

A shared cache also leaks timing. A hit returns faster than a miss, so one user might infer that someone else recently sent the same prefix. Whether a cache is shared per user, per organization or globally is a security decision as well as a performance one.

Design tests to separate allocation bugs, where a request gets the wrong blocks, from content bugs, where the right blocks hold the wrong values. Use lengths just below, at and just above a block boundary. Evict while a request is active, and fork from a partially filled block. Alternate two adapters over the same prompt IDs and compare each cached run with an uncached reference under the same adapter. A test that only confirms the lookup succeeded will pass in exactly the case where reuse is wrong.

The open questions are economic and statistical. Reuse is long-tailed: a few prefixes are read very often and most are read rarely, so eviction policy, TTL and the cost of storage compared with recomputation decide the outcome. Hit rate is the wrong objective on its own. What counts is prefill time saved, net of lookup and transfer, measured as time to first token on real traffic.

LESSONS.title: Compressed attention, sliding windows and replay
LESSONS.goal: Understand what changes when a model compresses, shares or reconstructs its attention state.
LESSONS.recall: Why is the conventional KV formula not universal?
LESSONS.predict: If each layer sees the last 128 tokens, is the entire multi-layer model’s dependence limited to 128 original tokens?
example: An engineer argues that because each layer attends over 128 tokens, replaying the last 128 raw tokens restores a 20-layer model exactly. What is missing?
Take the first token in the replayed region. In the original run, its deeper representations absorbed information that reached it, layer by layer, from positions before the replay boundary.

A replay that starts at the boundary has no access to that upstream state, so it can compute a different deeper representation. The tensors keep their dimensions while the lost information stays lost.

Exactness has to be established separately. Compare the replayed computation with the full reference on identical continuations, including boundary and long-context cases. If an approximation is acceptable, also evaluate the tasks you intend to serve.

questions.prompt: MLA, paging and SWA primarily concern…
options: They all describe the same memory-allocation technique.
They concern what is stored, how memory is organized, and which positions can be read.
They only change how text is split into tokens.
questions.why: Each term answers a different question: what is stored, how memory is organized and which positions can be read. A smaller cache can come from any of them, and each makes a different promise.
questions.hint: Ask a different question for each term.
option_feedback: Only paging is about allocation. MLA changes the representation, and SWA changes visibility.
Right. MLA changes the stored representation, paging organizes memory and SWA limits which positions a query reads.
Tokenization happens before any of these; all three concern attention state.

questions.prompt: An input has L = 10,000 tokens. Block hits come in multiples of 128, the hit may not exceed L − 134, and the saved sliding-window state for the last hit block is missing. What hit length does DeepInfer's policy use?
options: 9,866 tokens
9,856 tokens
9,728 tokens
questions.why: The cap is 9,866, which rounds down to a block hit of 9,856. Without window state for that block, the policy backs off one block to 9,728 and replays it.
questions.hint: Apply the cap, round down to a block, then ask what the missing state costs.
option_feedback: 9,866 is the cap and not a multiple of 128.
9,856 would be right if the window state were present.
Right. Missing window state means backing off one 128-token block and replaying it.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer's level-2 YoCo check finds that mask and compact modes produce matching log probabilities. What does this establish?
options: Bounded replay matches the full computation with truncation off
The two truncation implementations agree on the tested trajectories and configuration
Truncation is safe for any fine-tuned model
questions.why: Both compared modes truncate. The check proves equivalence between them, not between truncation and the untruncated reference.
questions.hint: Identify the two things actually compared.
option_feedback: Neither run had truncation off, so the gap from the full computation was never measured.
Right. Agreement holds for those two implementations, under the conditions tested.
Compatibility depends on layer topology, which this check takes as given.

transfer: Why would you avoid turning on a model-specific cache shortcut for an arbitrary model you fine-tuned?
Names architecture/config dependency
Distinguishes exactness from approximation
Requires reference and task-quality comparison

A shortcut can depend on how one architecture produces and consumes state, and a model I fine-tuned may not share those layer-sharing or attention dependencies. I would first establish compatibility, then find out whether the shortcut promises an exact calculation or accepts an approximation. I would compare it against the appropriate reference, test boundary and long-context cases, and evaluate task quality wherever numerical differences are allowed.
LESSONS.takeaway: A smaller cache can come from a different representation, narrower visibility or an approximation, and each makes a different promise.

levels.1:
So far we have pictured the KV cache as a key and a value saved for every layer and every position. That picture is a good starting point, but model designers are free to change what gets stored and how later layers use it.

Those choices matter to anyone working on an engine. A memory-saving trick that is valid for one architecture can be invalid for another, even when both are called transformers.

Compression changes what is stored. Multi-head latent attention (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek’s V2 paper, caches a compressed latent vector for each position, and the layer derives its keys and values from that vector. This changes how the model represents attention information. Paging is a separate matter; it only decides where allocated blocks live.

A window changes what a query can read directly. Sliding-window attention (SWA) limits each position to a recent stretch of the sequence. A layer might let a query read only the last 128 positions, which bounds some of the attention work and some of the stored state.

Layers build on one another, though. A recent position’s representation may already carry information that earlier layers pulled in from older positions. A 128-position window in every layer does not mean the model has forgotten everything more than 128 tokens back.

Sharing changes which layers must do their own work. Some architectures let later layers consume state that earlier layers produced. Yutao Sun and colleagues’ 2024 paper “You Only Cache Once” (YOCO) is the historical background for this kind of design. DeepInfer has its own model-specific producer and consumer layer paths, and their meaning comes from the configuration of the model they support.

Replaying a short segment can be an approximation. DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A describes rebuilding local sliding-window state by replaying a recent 128-token segment with truncated visibility, and it says plainly that the reconstruction is approximate. The replay deliberately skips rebuilding every upstream dependency.

That can be a sound engineering tradeoff, and it raises a specific question: how much does the difference affect the task? Showing that two implementations of the same shortcut agree is a separate result from showing that the shortcut matches the full original computation.

When reading this code, track for each path what is stored, what is reused and what is recomputed. Then pick a numerical or task-level comparison that tests the promise the path actually makes.
levels.2:
Begin with the reach of a stack of windows. If every layer lets position i read positions i−W+1 through i, then after k layers, information from up to k × W positions back can have reached position i. Mistral 7B's paper does this arithmetic for its own design: 32 layers with a 4,096-token window give a theoretical attention span of about 131K tokens. DeepSeek's deployment Q&A makes the same point about V4.1's decoder. Rebuilding its sliding-window state exactly would mean running the last 2,560 tokens through 20 decoder layers, which is 20 layers × 128 tokens. A short window bounds what each layer reads; it does not bound what the model depends on.

V4.1 keeps three kinds of attention state, and deepinfer/worker/cache_engine.py allocates each one separately. The paged block cache holds compressed latent entries, 528 bytes per entry in MXFP8, and _kv_bytes_per_token checks that the latent width plus the rotary width matches that layout. For comparison, one layer of the Llama-shaped model from the previous lesson stores 2 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 4,096 bytes per token, nearly eight times more, before V4.1's further compression across positions. An indexer cache holds small FP4 keys that let sparse attention pick which blocks to read. A per-sequence state slot holds the sliding-window keys and values for the most recent 134 positions of each windowed layer.

Layer sharing follows the YOCO pattern. In v4_modules/yoco.py, yoco_enabled is true when the configuration's n_prefill_layer is smaller than the total layer count. Layers from n_prefill_layer onward are consumer layers. They project their block KV from a shared hidden state taken at the first consumer layer, so prefill has to run the full prompt only through the producer layers. The consumer layers still need their own sliding-window state, and that is where truncation comes in.

DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE has three settings. off computes everything. mask keeps every query row but narrows the window so that keys before the retained suffix are invisible. compact removes the truncated query rows altogether. yoco_boundary_compact gathers the kept positions, and compact_yoco_boundary resets cross-layer metadata that described the old row layout. The retained suffix is DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS. It must be at least the window plus the backtracking allowance, so the README's default is 140 tokens, which covers 128 + 6. Mask and compact compute the same function on fewer rows, so they should agree. Both differ from off, because both drop the dependency path described in the first paragraph.

The replay rule itself, as the Q&A states it: replaying from position s, the query at position i attends only to keys from max(s, i−127) through i. The cost becomes a constant, independent of context length and layer count, and the resulting state is approximate.

Prefix hits follow from these pieces. For an input of length L, the hit may not exceed L − 134 tokens. The block cache is queried first and returns a hit L1 that is a multiple of 128. If saved window state exists between L1 − 128 and L1, the hit is L1; otherwise it is L1 − 128, and that last block is replayed. Take L = 10,000. The cap is 9,866, so L1 = 77 × 128 = 9,856. With window state present, the engine computes 144 new tokens. Without it, the hit falls to 9,728 and the engine computes 272, the first 128 of which only rebuild window state while the block KV is reused unchanged.
levels.3:
Each of these shortcuts has its own lineage. Noam Shazeer's multi-query attention (2019) made all query heads share one key/value head. Joshua Ainslie and colleagues' grouped-query attention (2023) kept a few shared heads. Both are architectural choices that must be made when the model is trained. DeepSeek-V2 (2024) introduced multi-head latent attention, storing a low-rank latent from which keys and values are derived. The authors reported a 93.3% smaller KV cache and up to 5.76× higher maximum generation throughput than their earlier 67B dense model. V2 is the historical source for MLA, not a specification of V4.1.

Windows have a parallel history. Iz Beltagy, Matthew Peters and Arman Cohan's Longformer (2020) combined local windows with a few global tokens. Mistral 7B (2023) used pure sliding windows and the layer-stacking argument for reach. Guangxuan Xiao and colleagues' StreamingLLM (2023) found that a window alone fails once the first tokens fall out of it, because models dump attention onto those early "sink" tokens. Keeping a handful of them restored stable generation. That result is a warning for any truncation scheme: which positions a model actually relies on is an empirical property of the trained weights, and a design diagram does not settle it. Cache eviction methods such as H2O (Zhenyu Zhang and colleagues, 2023) go further and drop entries judged unimportant. These are approximations, and their quality loss depends on the task.

Cross-layer sharing comes from Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Furu Wei and colleagues' "You Only Cache Once" (2024). There, a self-decoder produces one global KV cache that a cross-decoder reuses, so prefill can stop early. William Brandon and colleagues' Cross-Layer Attention (2024) shares KV between adjacent layers instead. DeepInfer's bounded replay is a separate idea layered on a YOCO-style model. It shortens the consumer layers' window rebuild and accepts that the result is approximate. The Q&A says decoder bounded replay nearly halves total prefill computation. It gives no task-quality numbers for the approximation, so that claim is about cost only.

The equivalence checks in examples/yoco/README.md show how far each test reaches. The level-1 check runs on one device in seconds without weights and compares window pivots, visible keys, store slots and compressed key ranges between mask and compact. The level-2 check needs 8 devices and a compatible V4.1 checkpoint, feeds both modes a fixed teacher-forcing trajectory and compares log probabilities and top-K entries one by one. Every other DEEPINFER_* variable must match between the two runs. Both levels test that two implementations of truncation agree. Neither compares truncation with off. To measure what the approximation costs, run off and compact on the same trajectories, report the log-probability gap by position relative to the replay boundary, and then evaluate long-context tasks whose answers depend on text far before the boundary.

Compatibility is the practical trap. These paths assume a particular layer topology: n_prefill_layer, which layers use windows, which layers share KV. The equivalence script refuses checkpoints that do not satisfy n_prefill_layer < n_layer. A fine-tune of V4.1 keeps that topology. A different architecture does not, even if its configuration file looks similar.

Open problems sit where model design and serving meet. Should an architecture be trained with the serving approximation in place, so that the approximation becomes exact by construction? How large a quality budget should a replay or eviction scheme be allowed, and on which tasks should it be checked? And which tests detect long-range dependencies that ordinary benchmarks rarely exercise?

LESSONS.title: MoE, parallelism and the slowest worker
LESSONS.goal: Explain what multiple GPUs share, what they split, and why one busy worker can delay the rest.
LESSONS.recall: What is the difference between total parameters and parameters used by one token?
LESSONS.predict: If half the tokens choose experts on one GPU, do equal expert counts guarantee balanced work?
example: Four devices finish their required work in 5, 5, 5 and 15 milliseconds, then synchronize. When can the group continue?
At 5 milliseconds three devices are ready. Their local work is done, while the fourth device is still computing something the next group operation needs.
The average completion time is 7.5 milliseconds, and the dependency takes no notice of averages. The group continues at 15 milliseconds, when the fourth device finishes.

The next question is why that device is slower. It might have hotter experts, more tokens, slower links or differently sized operations. Moving or replicating the right work could help, while adding devices without finding the cause might change nothing.

questions.prompt: Which scheme puts different experts on different GPUs?
options: Expert parallelism
Tensor parallelism
Changing the sampling temperature
questions.why: Expert parallelism assigns ownership of experts to devices and routes each token to the owners of its chosen experts.
questions.hint: Name the object being split.
option_feedback: Right. EP gives each device its own set of experts and sends tokens to them.
Tensor parallelism splits the matrices of one operation across devices, so every device takes part in every token’s operation.
Temperature changes how tokens are sampled and has nothing to do with where weights live.

questions.prompt: One logical expert receives 30% of a layer's tokens. EPLB places a second physical copy of it on another rank. What changes?
options: The model gains a new learned function for the router to choose
That expert's tokens can be split between two copies, while the number of logical experts stays the same
The router now picks from physical experts, so routing decisions change
questions.why: A redundant copy adds capacity for an existing logical expert. The gate still selects among logical experts; the copy only changes where the work runs.
questions.hint: Separate the function the router chooses from where its weights live.
option_feedback: A copy has identical weights, so it adds no new function.
Right. Logical experts are unchanged; the physical copies share their demand.
The gate selects logical experts; the logical-to-physical map decides which copy serves a token.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek reports moe_lb = 1.090 for decode, where moe_lb is the slowest rank's MoE load divided by the mean. What is the most defensible reading?
options: EP64 decode is 9% faster than EP8 decode
If MoE time is proportional to load, perfect balance could shorten that phase by at most about 8%
About 9% of routed tokens are dropped
questions.why: The barrier waits for the slowest rank at 1.09 × mean; perfect balance would bring it to the mean, saving 1 − 1/1.09 ≈ 8% of that phase under the proportionality assumption.
questions.hint: What does a barrier wait for, and what would perfect balance change?
option_feedback: The ratio compares ranks within one deployment, not two deployment sizes.
Right. It bounds what better balance could recover, under a stated assumption.
Inference does not drop routed tokens; the ratio measures uneven load.

transfer: An expert model gets little faster when you double its GPU count. Suggest two possible causes and how you would investigate them.
Includes routing skew or small expert batches
Includes communication/topology
Names a measurement per hypothesis

The router might send a disproportionate share of tokens to a few experts, so some devices finish early and wait. I would measure token demand and execution time per expert and per device. Communication might also grow more expensive as the group grows, especially across slower links between machines, so I would measure those transfers and inspect where the experts are placed.
LESSONS.takeaway: More devices help only when the useful work and the communication between them are organized to benefit.

levels.1:
“Run it on more GPUs” leaves the real design question open. With several devices, you have to decide which one stores which weights and which one does which work, and every choice brings its own communication. Before memorizing the abbreviations, ask what is being divided.

Data parallelism divides independent requests or tokens among devices. Tensor parallelism splits a single numerical operation, such as one large matrix multiplication, across devices. Pipeline parallelism gives different layers to different devices. Context parallelism splits the work on one long sequence. Each name tells you what gets split.

A mixture of experts (MoE) adds another kind of division. The model contains many feed-forward networks called experts, and for each token a router picks a small subset of them. All the experts’ weights exist, but any one token uses only a few.

That reduces the arithmetic per token, yet every expert’s weights still have to be stored somewhere. With expert parallelism (EP), different devices own different experts. Each token travels to the devices that hold its chosen experts, and the results travel back to be combined.

Equal storage does not guarantee equal work. Imagine four devices that each hold the same number of experts. If the router keeps choosing experts on one device, that device receives far more tokens than the others, which finish early and sit waiting for it.

Engine developers therefore measure demand per expert and time per device instead of counting experts. The links between devices matter too, because a fast connection inside one machine behaves very differently from a slower one between machines.

One remedy for a hot expert is to place extra copies of its weights on other devices so they can share the demand. DeepInfer’s expert containers keep the bookkeeping straight by separating logical experts, the learned functions the router selects, from physical placements, which include redundant copies. A copy adds capacity without adding a new learned function.

Copies cost memory and may require weights to be moved between devices. Larger device groups add coordination costs as well. A good design weighs those costs against the waiting it saves.

When you judge a multi-GPU result, start by drawing where the data lives and how it moves. A device count on its own explains very little.
levels.2:
Each way of splitting work has its own communication. Tensor parallelism splits a layer's matrices, so the partial results must be summed across devices (an all-reduce) inside every layer. Expert parallelism moves tokens instead. After the router picks experts, a dispatch sends each token's hidden vector to the ranks that own those experts, and a combine brings the weighted results back. DeepSeek's Q&A pairs expert parallelism with data-parallel attention, with as many data-parallel groups as expert-parallel ranks. Each rank runs attention only for its own requests, so their KV caches are never replicated, and then all ranks meet in the MoE layer. Prefill uses EP2–8. Decode uses EP64–128, which DeepSeek calls Wide-EP. Tensor and context parallelism are not used for now.

The reason to go wide in decode is batch size per expert. Take a model with 256 routed experts and 8 chosen per token, the routing shape DeepSeek-V3 used. At 60 sequences per rank, an EP8 group processes 480 tokens per step, which comes to 480 × 8 / 256 = 15 tokens per expert on average. An expert's matrix multiplication with 15 rows is limited by reading the expert's weights, not by arithmetic. At EP64 the group holds 3,840 tokens, or 120 per expert, and each rank also stores far fewer experts, so it reads fewer weight bytes per step. These numbers ignore draft tokens, which multiply the token count further.

The containers in v4_modules/moe.py keep four counts apart. logical is n_routed_experts, the range the gate selects from. extra is the number of redundant copies. physical = logical + extra, and it must divide evenly by ep_size. local = physical / ep_size, the experts held by one rank. resolve_num_extra_experts in model_executor/eplb rounds the extra count up until the division is exact. The gate, TopKGate, uses a learned correction bias (e_score_correction_bias, with a separate bias for image tokens) that shifts which experts are selected. This is DeepSeek's auxiliary-loss-free balancing, built into the model.

At run time, ExpertLoadBalancer counts tokens per physical expert at every step and keeps logical_to_physical_map, so a hot expert's tokens can be split among its copies. Every M steps, policy.py recomputes the placement. The objective for each layer, as stated in its comments, is to minimize the sum over recent steps of the largest load on any rank. The algorithm is greedy: experts are taken in descending order of load, and each is placed on the rank that increases that sum least. The new weights are then shuffled between GPUs over NVLink symmetric memory. The Q&A gives the production settings. Prefill starts from 4 redundant experts per GPU, with a 100-step statistics window and a reshuffle every 1,000 steps. Decode starts from 1 per GPU, with a 1,000-step window and a reshuffle every 10,000 steps.

The quality of the balance is reported as moe_lb, the slowest rank's load divided by the mean. The Q&A gives 1.074 for EP4DP4 prefill, 1.045 for EP2DP2 prefill and 1.090 for decode. In the 5, 5, 5, 15 ms example the ratio is 15 / 7.5 = 2.0. If MoE time grows in proportion to load, a ratio of 1.09 means perfect balance could cut the MoE phase by at most 1 − 1/1.09, about 8%.

Synchronization also reaches beyond the MoE layer. Every data-parallel rank must run the same kind of step, because all of them join the same dispatch and combine. That is why the scheduler votes on prefill versus decode, and why an idle rank runs an empty placeholder step instead of skipping ahead.
levels.3:
The parallelism vocabulary comes from training. Mohammad Shoeybi and colleagues' Megatron-LM (2019) split transformer matrices across GPUs with one all-reduce per block. Yanping Huang and colleagues' GPipe (2019) split layers into pipeline stages fed with micro-batches. Experts arrived through Dmitry Lepikhin and colleagues' GShard (2020) and William Fedus, Barret Zoph and Noam Shazeer's Switch Transformer (2021). Switch Transformer introduced the capacity factor, a cap on tokens per expert above which extra tokens are dropped, together with an auxiliary loss that pushes the router toward balance. DeepSeek later replaced that loss with a bias term that adjusts selection directly (Lean Wang and colleagues, 2024), the mechanism behind e_score_correction_bias. Inference inherits all of this, with a different objective: no tokens can be dropped, and the latency of each step matters.

The evidence for Wide-EP is DeepSeek's own. The Q&A shows an EP8-versus-EP64 throughput chart from the repository's offline benchmark script. It reports that production load balancing reaches roughly 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark, and gives the moe_lb ratios above. These figures are author-reported and have not been reproduced independently. They also come from one model and one hardware generation (SM100 GPUs inside one scale-up domain for the published benchmarks). Read the 80% figure as an estimate of what imbalance and routing cost in their traffic, not as a property of expert parallelism in general.

Large groups enlarge the failure domain. The Q&A states that all GPUs in an instance form one communication domain, so one failed GPU makes the whole instance unusable. On restart, the platform sets the EP size to however many healthy GPUs it actually receives, and restarts take minutes, so fault tolerance comes from spare capacity and rerouting requests. Long-running requests also hold a large group in place. A decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets a one-minute grace period, after which its unfinished requests and their KV caches are forwarded to other engines. The smallest efficient deployment is about 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs. Any proposal for wide expert parallelism has to accept that operating floor.

Balancing also interacts with numerics. In parallel_utils/userbuffer.py, DeepInfer turns off DeepEP's multiple-reduction mode when batch invariance is enabled together with periodic expert rearrangement. When expert copies move, the order in which partial results are summed can change, and with it the floating-point result. Changing placement for speed can therefore change outputs at the bit level. Anyone promising batch-invariant results has to account for it.

Topology decides more than device count does. The Q&A says the Mega MoE kernel is the general choice within a scale-up domain at any EP or batch size. Crossing machines means slower RDMA links, and the dispatch-and-combine traffic grows with tokens × top-k × hidden size. Before trusting a scaling chart, draw where experts live, how many bytes cross which links per step, and which collective waits for whom.

Several questions remain open. Placement uses load statistics from the last 100 to 1,000 steps, so it lags shifts in traffic, and how quickly it should react trades shuffle cost against imbalance. Speculative decoding multiplies tokens per step and changes how they are routed. Image and text tokens route differently, which is why the gate has two biases, so a mixed workload can be unbalanced in ways neither kind of traffic shows alone. And mean-based balance metrics can hide tail steps where one rank stalls everyone else.

LESSONS.title: Speculative decoding and DSpark
LESSONS.goal: Explain how guessing several tokens can save time without letting the guesses replace the target model.
LESSONS.recall: What prevents ordinary autoregressive generation from predicting many unknown steps independently?
LESSONS.predict: If draft length doubles, must accepted tokens per second double?
example: Two proposed tokens each have a 50% conditional acceptance rate. How many accepted draft tokens do you expect?
The first token is accepted in half the cases, so it contributes 0.5 tokens on average.

The second token counts only when the first survives and the second then survives too, which happens with probability 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Adding 0.5 for it directly would forget that it needs the first.

Add the contributions: 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 accepted draft tokens on average, before counting the target’s correction or bonus token. Choosing a fast setting still requires the time spent producing and checking the proposals.

questions.prompt: Why verify a draft with the target model?
options: To preserve the target’s intended generation behavior
To avoid loading target weights forever
To train the tokenizer
questions.why: Drafts are proposals. The target remains the reference for what the output should be.
questions.hint: Who decides what output is acceptable?
option_feedback: Right. Verification keeps the output faithful to the target model.
The target’s weights are used in every verification pass, so speculation never retires them.
Speculation happens at inference time and leaves the tokenizer unchanged.

questions.prompt: The drafter gives token a probability q(a) = 0.9 and the target gives it p(a) = 0.6. Under exact speculative sampling, with what probability is a drafted a accepted?
options: About 0.667
questions.why: Acceptance is min(1, p(a)/q(a)) = 0.6/0.9 ≈ 0.667. Combined with the drafter's 0.9 chance of proposing a, a is emitted with probability 0.6, exactly the target's.
questions.hint: The rule compares the two distributions as a ratio.
option_feedback: 0.6 is the overall probability of emitting a, after multiplying by the chance of drafting it.
0.9 is how often the drafter proposes a, and accepting all of them would overproduce a.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek's table shows dynamic-length verification at −1.5% throughput at 16 sequences per rank but +11.0% at 96. What best explains the pattern?
options: The confidence head is less accurate when few requests are active
At low concurrency a decode step is memory-bound, so extra verified positions are nearly free; at high concurrency each one costs compute other requests could use
Dynamic verification changes the output distribution more at high concurrency
questions.why: Trimming verification saves work only when that work has a cost. At low load, verification rides on the weight reads that the step pays for anyway.
questions.hint: When does verifying one more position actually cost time?
option_feedback: The table shows accepted length barely changing at any concurrency, so calibration is not the explanation.
Right. The value of trimming depends on whether the step is memory-bound or compute-bound.
Exact verification preserves the target distribution at any length; throughput is what changes.

transfer: Explain how longer drafts could help one user receive tokens faster but reduce the amount of useful work the server does for everyone.
Names saved serial rounds
Names added low-value verification work
Includes concurrency or capacity constraint

A single user may advance through several accepted tokens in one target-model round, which cuts the number of serial waits. Later draft positions have to survive every earlier position, though, so some of the extra checking has little chance of helping. With many requests active, that verification consumes capacity that could serve other users. I would measure accepted progress, drafting and checking time, and latency at the intended concurrency before settling on a draft length.
LESSONS.takeaway: Drafting pays off when the accepted progress is worth more than the work of drafting and verifying it.

levels.1:
In ordinary generation, the model has to choose the next token before it knows the input for the prediction after that. Each round runs the full model, and the rounds happen one after another, so their cost limits how quickly a single person receives an answer.

Speculative decoding, which Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias formalized in 2022, gets more progress out of each round of the main model, called the target. A cheaper drafter proposes several tokens, and the target evaluates all of the proposed positions in a single pass.

The target then checks the proposal. It accepts some draft tokens and corrects the first rejected position. The acceptance rule matters here. Exact speculative sampling, as Leviathan and colleagues define it, preserves the target’s output probability distribution as long as the algorithm’s assumptions hold.

That promise does not mean two implementations will print the same string for the same seed. Two draws from one valid distribution can differ, so matching a distribution and matching one particular random run are different properties.

Later guesses depend on earlier ones surviving. Suppose the drafter proposes three tokens. The third becomes part of the answer only if the first two were accepted as well, so you cannot count each position as if it contributed on its own.

That makes the length of a draft a gamble. A long draft offers a chance to advance far in one round, but its later positions are unlikely to survive, and checking them still uses work that could have served another request.

DeepSeek’s DSpark paper makes that budget choice deliberately. It pairs a draft design with confidence-based verification scheduling. The system estimates how likely each proposed prefix is to survive and weighs that against how its hardware performs at different amounts of verification work.

DeepInfer contains a related scheduling path that turns confidence estimates into a work length for each request. The draft-length experiment here isolates the intuition behind that choice and does not reproduce the full production scheduler.

To evaluate speculation on your own model, measure the useful tokens accepted per round together with the time spent drafting and checking them. A high acceptance rate alone does not prove a speedup, and a setting that helps one user may waste capacity when many users are active.
levels.2:
Write a_j for the probability that draft position j survives, given that every earlier position survived. Position j contributes an accepted token only if all positions up to j survive, so the expected number of accepted drafts is Σᵢ Πⱼ≤ᵢ aⱼ. If every a_j equals the same α and the draft has γ positions, the sum simplifies. Leviathan and colleagues add the one token the target always contributes (a correction at the first rejection, or a bonus token after a fully accepted draft) and get (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α) tokens per target round. With α = 0.8, a 2-token draft yields (1 − 0.512) / 0.2 = 2.44 tokens per round, and a 5-token draft yields (1 − 0.262) / 0.2 ≈ 3.69. The fifth position adds only 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.33 expected tokens, yet it costs as much to verify as the first.

The acceptance rule keeps the target's distribution intact. A draft token x drawn from the drafter's distribution q is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target's distribution. On rejection, the replacement is drawn from max(0, p − q), renormalized. A two-token vocabulary shows that this works. Let q(a) = 0.9, q(b) = 0.1, p(a) = 0.6 and p(b) = 0.4. A drafted a survives with probability 0.6 / 0.9 ≈ 0.667, so a is emitted with probability 0.9 × 0.667 = 0.6. A drafted b always survives, since p(b) exceeds q(b). The residual is (0, 0.3), which renormalizes to all-b, so every rejection emits b. The probability of b is then 0.1 + 0.9 × 0.333 = 0.4. Both outputs match p exactly. Greedy verification is the special case where the target's distribution puts all its weight on its top token.

In DeepInfer the verification lives in Sampler._verification (model_executor/layers/sampler.py). prepare_verification_metadata maps each row of logits to its request and draft step. Structured-output masks are applied to every step, then process_sampling compares each draft token's log probability under the drafter, stored in the MTP info pool from the previous round, with the target's. get_accept_result finds each request's accepted prefix, and finalize_verification packs the accepted and sampled tokens. After sampling, the draft head (DFlash in this code) runs on the output token to propose the next round's drafts and their confidences. The docstring points out a read-after-write dependency across steps: this round's verification reads what the previous round's draft pass wrote to the pool, and only stream order keeps that safe.

The confidence scheduler decides how many positions each request verifies. MtpVarlen::schedule in csrc/engine/mtp_varlen.hpp gathers every (survival estimate, request) pair and sorts them in descending order. It starts from one mandatory token per request and adds candidates one at a time, raising the expected output by each candidate's estimate. At each size it predicts step time from a measured curve, baseline_ms for that graph size plus a fitted slope and an estimate of sampler time, and it keeps the size with the highest expected tokens per millisecond. Each request then verifies one token plus as many of its own candidates as made the cut. Under asynchronous scheduling the CPU fixes only the total, using estimates two rounds old. The TileLang kernel in schedule_mtp_varlen.py recomputes the survival products from the latest confidences on the GPU, ranks all request–position pairs, and gives each request the number of its positions that rank inside the budget.

A small case shows the choice. Request A's survival estimates are 0.9, 0.8 and 0.6, and B's are 0.5, 0.2 and 0.1. With room for three extra positions, all three go to A, adding 2.3 expected tokens, and B verifies only its mandatory token. Whether three extra positions beat two depends on whether the 0.6 is worth the added step time on that hardware.
levels.3:
The idea predates the name. Mitchell Stern, Noam Shazeer and Jakob Uszkoreit's blockwise parallel decoding (2018) predicted several future tokens and checked them with the main model. Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman and Yossi Matias (ICML 2023) and, independently, Charlie Chen and colleagues at DeepMind (2023) added the rejection-sampling rule that keeps the target's distribution exact. Leviathan's group reported 2–3× speedups on T5-XXL, and Chen's group reported 2–2.5× on Chinchilla 70B. The drafter then got cheaper. Medusa (Tianle Cai and colleagues, 2024) attached extra decoding heads to the target. EAGLE (Yuhui Li and colleagues, 2024) drafted from the target's hidden features. SpecInfer (Xupeng Miao and colleagues) verified trees of candidates in one pass. DeepSeek-V3's report used its multi-token-prediction module as a drafter, with 85–90% acceptance of the second token and 1.8× tokens per second.

DSpark (Xin Cheng, Wenfeng Liang and colleagues, 2026) changes both halves. The drafter is semi-autoregressive: a parallel drafter paired with a light sequential module that models dependencies between drafted tokens. Verification is scheduled by confidence and by a profile of hardware throughput. The authors report that, deployed in the DeepSeek-V4 serving system, it speeds up per-user generation by 60–85% over the production MTP-1 baseline at matched throughput. As with any vendor result, the drafter, traffic mix and hardware are theirs, and the comparison is against their own earlier system.

The Q&A isolates the scheduling half. Against fixed 5-token verification, dynamic lengths cut verified tokens per step from 5 to between 3.24 and 4.44 while barely moving accepted length (3.29 versus 3.20 on average). The estimated throughput change depends strongly on concurrency: −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. The pattern fits the roofline picture. At low concurrency a decode step is limited by memory, so extra verified positions are almost free and trimming them loses accepted tokens for nothing. At high concurrency each verified position costs real compute that other requests could use. Note the word "estimated": the Q&A computes these figures from EP64/DP64 benchmark data, so they come from a model of throughput, not a measured end-to-end A/B test.

Several things break the scheme. A confidence head that is overconfident sends verification to tokens that will be rejected. DeepInfer's verification path computes a batch_confidence_error, an obvious quantity to monitor. Distribution exactness holds only if the draft and target distributions are processed identically, with the same temperature, top-k or top-p truncation and grammar mask at every position. The sampler applies structured-output masks to every draft step for this reason. A stop token proposed inside a draft must end the sequence at that point. Determinism is a further casualty. DeepInfer's README requires DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 for deterministic sampling. A plausible reason is that the varlen budget is shared across the batch, so a request's verified length depends on its companions. The README states the requirement but not the reason.

When evaluating a speculative setup, report accepted tokens per target round, the time to draft and to verify, inter-token latency percentiles and total throughput at the concurrency you will serve. Report how acceptance varies by task too, since code and prose are drafted with different success. The open problems are calibration under distribution shift, drafters for fine-tuned targets (a drafter trained on the base model may lose acceptance after fine-tuning), and joint scheduling of draft length with batch size when both compete for the same step budget.

LESSONS.title: Correctness, determinism and structured output
LESSONS.goal: Choose a check that tests the specific kind of correctness your change promises.
LESSONS.recall: How does equal output distribution differ from identical outputs?
LESSONS.predict: If JSON parses successfully, have you proved the answer’s facts are true?
example: A cache change produces valid JSON, but its numerical predictions disagree with the reference at a page boundary. Would you accept an exactness claim?
Valid JSON shows that the output followed a structural constraint. It says nothing about whether attention read the right positions or the right cached values.

The disagreement on identical prefixes bears directly on the claimed numerical equivalence. Find the first position and layer where the values differ, starting near the page boundary where the error shows up.

Fix that mismatch before accepting the exactness claim. If an approximation is acceptable instead, state that different contract and test its effect on real task quality. Valid formatting cannot stand in for either check.

questions.prompt: A JSON grammar proves…
options: Truth of every field
Conformance to the supported structural constraints
That no sampling occurs
questions.why: Structure and truth are different properties. A grammar constrains form and cannot check facts.
questions.hint: A perfectly formatted wrong answer is still possible.
option_feedback: A grammar constrains form, so a perfectly formatted field can still be false.
Right. The grammar guarantees that the output fits the structure it encodes.
Constrained decoding still samples; the grammar only masks out illegal tokens.

questions.prompt: A seed by itself guarantees batch invariance.
options: Yes
No, numerical execution and RNG assignment also matter
Only for long prompts
questions.why: Different batching can change the order of reductions or which random draw goes to which request, unless both are controlled.
questions.hint: What happens before random selection?
option_feedback: A seed fixes the random draws, yet batching can change the numbers those draws act on.
Right. Batch composition can change reduction order and the assignment of random draws.
Prompt length plays no special role; batch effects can appear at any length.

questions.prompt: Best first oracle for an exact attention-kernel rewrite?
options: Matching layer outputs against a reference over varied shapes
A user says responses feel good
An aggregate throughput chart
questions.why: Test the numerical claim at the operator boundary before measuring downstream behavior.
questions.hint: Pin the promised invariant directly.
option_feedback: Right. It tests the promised numerical equality directly, across the shapes where bugs hide.
User impressions cannot detect small numerical errors that matter later.
Throughput measures speed and says nothing about whether the outputs are correct.

transfer: Pick an engine change and describe what you would compare to decide whether it is correct. Say what the comparison would and would not establish.
Names a reference
States equality/tolerance/quality criterion
States tested configurations and boundaries

For a cache-read change, I would feed identical token prefixes to the full reference calculation and to the cached path, then compare the next-token scores within a stated tolerance. I would include cache boundaries and interleaved requests. That tests the numerical property directly under those conditions. It does not cover every possible configuration, and it says nothing about whether the model’s answers are factually correct, so those claims need their own checks.
LESSONS.takeaway: A test can pass while the property that matters goes untested. Match each check to the claim it supports.

activity.title: Check the numbers before judging a fluent answer.
activity.intro: Two paths receive the same fixed input IDs [1, 4]. The reference returns next-token scores [0.2, 0.8, -0.1]. A changed path returns [0.2, 0.805, -0.1]. Your stated rule permits an absolute difference of at most 0.001 in every score. Both paths still choose the second token when selecting the highest score.

fields.label: What is the largest absolute score difference?
fields.why: The second entry differs by 0.805 − 0.8 = 0.005. The other entries match.

fields.label: Does the changed path pass the stated numerical rule?
options: yes
Yes, because it chooses the same token
no
No, because one score difference exceeds the tolerance
fields.why: 0.005 is greater than 0.001. Matching the highest-scoring token does not establish that the numerical comparison passed.

activity.conclusion: A useful correctness check needs fixed inputs, a reference, a comparison rule and a boundary. Passing this one numerical case would still leave request isolation, stop behavior and task quality unchecked.

levels.1:
Suppose you change how a model reads its cache. The program runs, the response sounds fluent and its JSON parses. Has the change preserved the model’s calculation? Each observation is useful, and none of them answers that question.

An array can have the right dimensions and hold the wrong numbers. A paragraph can read well and still differ from what the reference model would have written.

JSON is a structured text format that programs can parse into fields and values. A grammar can restrict which continuations the sampler may choose, so that an answer follows the format. The grammar guarantees structure, and a perfectly formatted field can still hold the wrong date or an invented fact.

Start by naming the property you want to preserve. An exact attention rewrite should match a reference’s numerical outputs within a stated rounding tolerance. An exact sampling method should preserve a probability distribution. A deliberate approximation may differ numerically, as long as task quality stays within an agreed limit.

The trusted comparison path is called a reference, and it is often a simpler implementation. A check that tells you whether the property holds is sometimes called an oracle. The name does not make it infallible, so you still need to understand exactly what it checks.

Control the input when you compare outputs. If two generators pick different tokens, their later inputs differ too, and every difference after that point becomes hard to interpret.
