Feed both implementations the same known continuation instead, and compare their predictions at the same positions. This is called teacher forcing.

Teacher forcing lets you find the first disagreement before diverging histories bury its cause.

Some bugs never appear in a pleasant example. A cache bug might show up only when a sequence crosses a block boundary. A state leak might need two requests interleaved in a particular order. A sampling bug might appear only when a stop token is proposed inside a draft. Design the case that exercises the property instead of relying on an ordinary chat.

Deterministic sampling and batch invariance are separate promises. A seed controls the random draws. Batch invariance means a request’s output stays the same when its batch companions change, and that also depends on how the arithmetic is grouped. A seed alone does not make every numerical execution identical.

A good report states what the evidence establishes and names what it leaves open, such as task quality when only numbers were compared.
levels.2:
Floating-point addition is not associative, and that one fact explains most of the "same input, different output" surprises. In FP32, the spacing between representable numbers near 10⁸ is 8. So (10⁸ + 1) − 10⁸ evaluates to 0, while (10⁸ − 10⁸) + 1 evaluates to 1. A matrix multiplication or attention kernel sums thousands of products. If it splits that sum differently, for instance because a larger batch leads it to choose another tiling, the result changes in the last bits. Under greedy selection, a tiny change can swap two near-tied tokens, and every later token then follows a different history.

DeepInfer separates two promises here. Batch invariance, enabled with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 on NVIDIA only, means a request's numbers do not depend on its batch companions. In worker/runtime_config.py the flag switches DeepGEMM and TileKernels to deterministic algorithms. It passes batch_invariant to the attention backend and, in userbuffer.py, turns off DeepEP's multiple-reduction mode when experts are being rearranged. Deterministic sampling additionally needs a fixed seq_seed in SamplingParams and the confidence-varlen scheduler turned off. A seed fixes the random draws. Batch invariance fixes the numbers the draws act on. Each needs the other.

Teacher forcing is built into the sampler. golden_output holds forced tokens: wherever an entry is not −1, the sampler emits that token instead of its own choice, so two implementations can be run over one fixed trajectory. The YoCo equivalence check uses this to compare log probabilities and top-K entries position by position. A useful comparison reports the first position, and then the first layer, where the outputs differ beyond tolerance. Errors that begin at a cache-block boundary or the replay boundary point to a specific bug.

Structured output runs on a parallel track. DeepSeek's Q&A says schemas are compiled asynchronously into a grammar automaton on dedicated machines, and a request fetches the compiled result before entering the engine. At run time, Sampler._get_so_mask works through each constrained request. It advances the matcher by the tokens the previous step accepted, fills a vocabulary bitmask for the next position, then walks the matcher through each draft token in turn, filling a mask for every draft step until the matcher rejects one. Finally it calls matcher.rollback so the grammar state again matches the committed text. The masks hold one bit per vocabulary entry, about 16 KB per row for a vocabulary of 128,000. They are copied on a separate CUDA stream, and sampling waits on an event before applying them.

Failures are contained per request. A matcher exception marks only that request as failed (FINISHED_SO_FAILED), because raising an error on the sampling path would stall every request in the group. A structured-output request that gets preempted is stopped rather than recomputed, because its grammar state cannot be replayed.

For your own changes, choose the comparison that fits the claim. Use bitwise equality for batch invariance. For an exact kernel rewrite, compare elementwise within a stated tolerance on teacher-forced trajectories. For a speculative sampler, run a distribution test. For a grammar change, check every output with a separate parser and look for tokens the mask wrongly allowed or forbade, especially where a token's text spans a grammar boundary.
levels.3:
The clearest public evidence on nondeterminism comes from Horace He and colleagues at Thinking Machines Lab ("Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference", September 2025). They sampled 1,000 completions at temperature 0 from Qwen3-235B-A22B with the same prompt and got 80 distinct outputs; the most common appeared 78 times. With batch-invariant kernels, all 1,000 were identical. They argue that the usual explanation, concurrency plus floating point, is incomplete. A single forward pass is deterministic from run to run, but kernels choose a reduction strategy based on batch size, and a server's batch size changes with its load. The fix had a cost. On Qwen3-8B, 1,000 sequences took 26 s in default vLLM, 55 s with unoptimized deterministic kernels and 42 s with an improved attention kernel. Their batch-invariant matrix multiplication was about 20% slower than cuBLAS. DeepInfer's switch makes the same trade, and it is supported on NVIDIA only.

Why pay for it? One reason is debugging: without invariance, you cannot tell a real regression from batch-composition noise. Reinforcement learning is another. If the sampler and the trainer compute different probabilities for the same tokens, nominally on-policy training is quietly off-policy, and the Thinking Machines post makes that argument. Bitwise reproducibility across different hardware, such as NVIDIA and Ascend, is a separate and much harder goal than invariance on one platform.

Constrained decoding has its own literature. Brandon Willard and Rémi Louf (2023) compiled regular expressions into finite automata indexed over the vocabulary, which made masking cheap; their library is Outlines. Yixin Dong and colleagues' XGrammar (2024) handles context-free grammars with a pushdown automaton. It precomputes the many tokens whose legality does not depend on the stack, so only the rest are checked at run time. DeepInfer's sampler calls XGrammar for its bitmasks. Two cautions follow from this work. Grammars operate on characters while models emit subword tokens, so the mask is correct only if every token's whole text is checked against the grammar state. And a format constraint can change what the model says: Zhi Rui Tam and colleagues ("Let Me Speak Freely?", 2024) reported lower reasoning scores under strict format restrictions on some tasks. A grammar guarantees that the output parses, and the content still has to be evaluated.

Each kind of claim needs its own evidence. A tolerance should come from the number format: BF16 keeps 8 significant bits, so one rounding step contributes a relative error of up to about 0.4%, and long reductions accumulate more. Investigate structured mismatches even when they fall inside the tolerance. An exact sampler needs a statistical test. On a toy distribution, 100,000 draws estimate a probability of 0.5 with a standard error of about 0.0016, so a gap of 0.01 is a bug and not noise. An approximation, such as quantization, bounded replay or eviction, needs a task-quality budget declared before the measurement and checked on the tasks you serve.

The open problems are about coverage. Differential testing against a simple reference finds bugs only on the shapes and schedules it runs. Ideas from bounded model checking, which enumerates every case of a small configuration (every block-boundary offset, every interleaving of two requests, every position of a stop token inside a draft), catch the cases that ordinary prompts miss. Errors also compound over long generations in ways no single-step tolerance captures, so long teacher-forced trajectories, compared position by position, remain the most informative check for an exact rewrite.

LESSONS.title: From a fast engine to a usable service
LESSONS.goal: Trace the work that surrounds a model calculation, and judge when splitting prefill and decode across machines pays for itself.
LESSONS.recall: Which parts of an online service live outside the engine loop?
LESSONS.predict: Can putting prefill and decode on separate workers make a small workload slower?
example: Fetching a cached prefix from a remote store takes 18 milliseconds and saves 10 milliseconds of prefill. Does the cache hit help this request?

Start by comparing the time added with the time saved. If the fetch cannot overlap with anything else, the request pays 18 milliseconds to avoid 10, and finishes 8 milliseconds later than it would have without the cache.

The fetch might overlap with other useful work, such as time the request would have spent queued anyway. It might also compete with other requests for network bandwidth. Either could change the answer, so time the fetch and the prefill separately on real traffic.
Report user-visible latency next to the hit rate. A higher hit rate means more prefixes were found, and it helps only when using them makes requests finish sooner.

questions.prompt: Putting prefill and decode on different workers creates a need to…
options: Move compatible attention state from the prefill worker to the decode worker
Tokenize the prompt again on the decode worker so it can rebuild the context
Run a separately trained model on each worker
questions.why: Decode continues from the attention state that prefill computed, so that state has to reach the decode worker intact and in a format it can use.
questions.hint: What did prefill produce that decode consumes?
option_feedback: Right: the decode worker needs the keys and values prefill computed, and they have to arrive complete and compatible.
Token IDs alone would force the decode worker to redo the prefill that the split was meant to move elsewhere.
Both stages run the same model; disaggregation changes where the work happens, and the weights stay the same.

questions.prompt: DeepInfer’s scheduler refuses to start a decode-only (COMPLETION) engine unless preempted requests are stopped. Why?
options: Decode-only engines run one request at a time, so preemption would leave them idle
Stopping preempted requests keeps the sampling seed from changing between attempts
A decode-only engine has no prefill path, so it cannot rebuild an evicted request’s cache by recomputing it
questions.why: Recomputing a preempted request means prefilling its prompt and generated tokens again. A decode-only worker has no prefill channel, so the only local options are to stop the request or to send it back through a prefill worker.
questions.hint: What does the recompute branch of _preempt put the request through again?
option_feedback: Decode engines batch many requests; max_num_seqs sets that limit, and preemption exists precisely because several compete for blocks.
Seeds play no part in this check; it concerns whether the engine can rebuild cache state at all.
Right: recompute is a prefill, and a COMPLETION engine has no prefill channel to run it.

questions.prompt: Your team serves a few requests per second on eight GPUs and is considering splitting prefill and decode. Which evidence would best settle the decision?
options: Goodput under your latency targets on your traffic, comparing the split against a colocated engine with chunked prefill
DeepSeek’s reported tokens per day and revenue per GPU-hour, scaled down to eight GPUs
Peak throughput of the split system at its largest batch size, against a colocated engine serving one request at a time
questions.why: Disaggregation trades handoff cost for less interference. Goodput on your own traffic, against the strongest colocated alternative, measures that trade where you will operate.
questions.hint: Which comparison holds the workload and the strength of the alternative fixed?
option_feedback: Right: goodput captures both latency targets at once, and chunked prefill is the colocated design that already attacks the same interference.
Those figures are author-reported at a scale whose smallest efficient unit is 128 GPUs, and they do not scale down linearly.
Comparing a tuned peak against a deliberately weak baseline inflates the gain and ignores the latency targets entirely.

transfer: Describe a simple service for your fine-tuned model. Where does unfinished work live, and what should happen when a user cancels?
Identifies request queue and KV ownership
Includes model/tokenizer/adapter identity
Names cancellation/timeout handling

Requests first wait in a bounded queue and then run in a compatible engine. Each active request owns its working state, including its attention cache. The service records which base model, adapter and input format are in use. When a request completes or is cancelled, the service releases its slot and state once no consumer still needs them. I would get this simple path working before adding remote transfers or separately scaled stages.
LESSONS.takeaway: An engine becomes a usable service once queues, routing, state transfer and failure handling surround it.

levels.1:
A request spends only part of its life on the GPU.

A user types a question. Before any model calculation starts, a server has to receive it, check that the user may send it, turn the text into tokens, pick a worker, and perhaps hold the request until a slot frees up. When the model finishes, the token IDs are turned back into text and streamed to the user. Each of those steps can add delay, and each can fail.

That surrounding machinery is what turns an engine into a service. Keeping the two apart helps when you read a production architecture diagram. It also explains how an open-source engine can be fast and still fall short of something you could put in front of users. The DeepInfer README is explicit about which parts of DeepSeek’s internal service the release includes.

Large deployments can give each stage its own workers.

Prefill reads the whole known prompt in one pass. Decode then extends the answer one token at a time. The two load the hardware differently, so a large deployment can give each stage its own machines and its own scheduling. Running the stages apart like this is called disaggregation.

DeepSeek’s deployment Q&A describes a system that also gives multimodal encoding, the work of turning images into representations the model can read, a stage of its own. The stages still depend on one another. Decode cannot begin until it holds the numerical state that prefill produced.

Every split creates a handoff.

If one machine processes the prompt and another continues the answer, the attention state has to travel between them. The transfer uses network bandwidth, makes the request depend on a second machine, and opens one more place where something can go wrong.

For a large or uneven workload, scaling prompt work and answer work independently can repay those costs. A small workload may run better with both stages on one machine. Measurements of your own traffic are what settle which case you are in.

Queues hold work without adding capacity.

When requests arrive faster than the engine completes them, the unfinished ones pile up. If the queue may grow without limit, requests at the back wait longer and longer. A service needs a policy that says how much work to admit, how long a request may wait, and what happens when either limit is reached.

Requests also end early. A user closes the tab, or a timeout fires. The service has to notice and release that request’s memory and scheduler slot, or abandoned work keeps occupying space that live requests need.

Start with a system you can explain.

For a first service around your fine-tuned model, use one compatible engine and a workload that resembles your real traffic. Confirm that it loads the model you intended and behaves as expected. Then measure which step of the request’s journey is slow, before you copy an architecture built for a far larger load.
levels.2:
Count the requests in flight before drawing boxes.

Little’s law ties three quantities together for any stable queueing system: the average number of requests inside it equals the arrival rate times the average time each request spends there. If 20 requests arrive per second and each spends 6 seconds between arrival and its last streamed token, about 120 requests are in the system at any moment. Each one holds a scheduler slot or a queue position, and every running one holds attention cache memory.

Turn the law around to find capacity. Suppose the engine can run 64 requests at once and each takes 6 seconds of engine time. It completes about 64 / 6 ≈ 10.7 requests per second. At 20 arrivals per second the queue grows by roughly 9.3 requests every second, and no steady state exists. Every admission policy in a service is a decision about what to do with those 9.3: refuse them, let them wait against a deadline, or degrade what each request receives.

DeepInfer’s scheduler enforces two limits and one eviction rule.

The scheduler is C++ in csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp, driven from Python by LLMEngine.step. It reads max_num_seqs (how many requests may run at once) and max_num_batched_tokens (how many tokens one step may process). The offline example sets 4 and 32,768. A waiting request is admitted only while both limits leave room.

During decode, every running request needs space for its next tokens. When the block manager cannot allocate a block, _preempt evicts a request in one of two ways. With stop_preempted_request set, the request ends with status FINISHED_PREEMPTED. Otherwise reset_for_recompute clears its cache bookkeeping, the request goes back to the front of the waiting queue, and its prompt and generated tokens are prefilled again later. Requests under a structured-output grammar cannot be recomputed and are always stopped. The offline LLM wrapper defaults to recomputing.

Cancellation is an explicit call.

LLMEngine.abort_request passes request IDs to the scheduler’s abort_sequence, which scans both the running and waiting queues and marks matches FINISHED_ABORTED. The scheduler frees their blocks and slots on its next pass, and any image buffers the request held are returned to their shared pool. The engine docstring says plainly that the release has no online-serving wrapper. Whatever server you put in front of it has to notice a closed connection or an expired deadline and make this call, or the abandoned request keeps generating.

The disaggregation seams are visible and empty.

deepinfer/engine/engine_type.py defines three engine roles: NORMAL runs prompts and completions, PROMPT runs only prefill, and COMPLETION runs only decode. LLMEngine has hook methods such as init_pd_split, send_processed_prompts and pe_do_save_kvcache whose bodies are empty in this release. That matches the README, which lists prefill/decode disaggregation as missing while saying most of the engine functionality it needs is present.

One check in the scheduler’s constructor shows a cost of the split. A COMPLETION engine refuses to start unless stop_preempted_request is true, because it has no prefill channel. A decode-only worker that evicts a request cannot rebuild that request’s cache by itself. Recovery has to go back through a prefill worker, or the request fails.

Price the handoff with the numbers you have.

DeepSeek’s Q&A budgets about 400 Gbps of interconnect per 8 GPUs, which is 50 GB/s per machine, or about 6.25 GB/s for each GPU’s share. The SWA state DeepSeek stores per sequence is 20 layers × 134 tokens × 528 bytes = 1,415,040 bytes, about 0.23 milliseconds at that rate. The main block cache is far larger. As an invented illustration, a model with 50 KB of cache per token and a 32,768-token prompt would move about 1.6 GB, roughly 0.26 seconds, and that time lands on time to first token unless it overlaps with other work.

The Q&A also separates the parts of a cache hit by whether they can hide. Matching a prefix is a hash-chain lookup over metadata, and its result decides routing, so it sits on the critical path. Fetching cache blocks from storage into host shared memory runs asynchronously in another process. Swapping them into GPU memory runs layer by layer alongside the forward pass, using RDMA network cards so the copy does not occupy GPU compute units. Only the serial part adds directly to latency.
levels.3:
Disaggregation came from a measured interference problem.

The modern serving loop starts with Orca, by Gyeong-In Yu and colleagues (OSDI 2022), which scheduled at the granularity of one model iteration so that requests could join and leave a running batch. vLLM, from Woosuk Kwon and colleagues (SOSP 2023), added paged cache storage so that such batches could stay large without fragmenting memory. Twenty-one files in DeepInfer’s Python package carry a header saying they were derived from vLLM.

Once prefill and decode share a batch, a long prompt can stall every decoding request in the same step. DistServe, by Yinmin Zhong and colleagues (OSDI 2024), measured this interference and proposed separate prefill and decode instances. It also reframed the metric as goodput: the highest request rate at which a target fraction of requests meet both a time-to-first-token target and a per-token latency target. Splitwise, by Pratyush Patel and colleagues at Microsoft (ISCA 2024), split the phases onto different machine pools and considered different hardware for each. Mooncake, from Moonshot AI (Ruoyu Qin and colleagues, FAST 2025), organized the system around a disaggregated cache pool spread over host memory and SSDs.

The colocated alternative did not stand still. Sarathi-Serve, by Amey Agrawal and colleagues (OSDI 2024), splits prompts into chunks and mixes them with decode work so that no step stalls for long. DeepInfer’s prefill path does a version of this: its Q&A describes a fitted quadratic cost model that chooses each chunk’s size to use up a per-step time budget. The fair comparison for a new deployment is therefore disaggregated serving against a well-tuned colocated engine with chunked prefill, judged by goodput on your traffic. Peak throughput of either alone settles little.

Read DeepSeek’s numbers as one operating point.

The Q&A reports that a single cluster serves 155 trillion tokens per day, with revenue of US$38 per GPU-hour at off-peak pricing, and that its load balancers reach about 80% of a perfectly balanced offline benchmark. These are author-reported production figures, and the course has not reproduced them. They describe a design whose smallest efficient unit is 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs, with a roughly 1:1 GPU ratio between stages and decode spread across 64 to 128 GPUs with wide expert parallelism. The design is a strong argument about that scale and offers little guidance for an eight-GPU deployment.

Several of its choices depend on DeepSeek’s model. Prefill and decode can sit in different but adjacent data centers only because V4.1 Flash compresses its cache heavily. Routing ignores prefix affinity because every prefill machine reads from a shared storage cluster, so any machine can hit any prefix. A system whose cache lives on the GPU that computed it faces the opposite trade: sending a request to the machine that holds its prefix can overload that machine.

Failure handling is part of the architecture.

The Q&A treats restarts, which take minutes, as unavoidable. Reliability comes from spare quota and rerouting. A decode engine that receives a shutdown notice gets a one-minute grace period, then forwards its unfinished requests and their caches to other decode engines. Scale-in is forbidden while quota utilization is above 0.8. Because a large expert-parallel instance forms one communication domain, one failed GPU disables the instance, and on restart the platform rebuilds it at whatever expert-parallel size the healthy GPUs allow. Llumnix, by Biao Sun and colleagues (OSDI 2024), studied live migration of running requests between instances as a general scheduling tool; DeepSeek’s forwarding at shutdown is a narrower use of the same capability.

Cache retention is an economic choice with measured costs. The Q&A gives a three-day lifetime for agent traffic and seven days for chatbot traffic, and reports that a three-day lifetime costs chatbot traffic 0.5 to 1 percentage point of hit rate, because a few chatbot prefixes are read very many times over a long period.

Open problems remain at every boundary. Cache keys must carry model and adapter identity as models change under a running fleet. Load balancers must weigh request count against total cache length, which the Q&A says its decode balancer does heuristically. And goodput under bursty arrivals, the regime where queue policy matters most, is the least reported number in the literature.

LESSONS.title: Read DeepInfer without getting lost
LESSONS.goal: Follow one request through DeepInfer before studying any single optimization.
LESSONS.recall: What evidence separates an engine feature from a production service feature?
LESSONS.predict: Will reading every kernel before the request loop give you the clearest first map?
example: You find an output clone inside the generation loop. How do you decide whether it is needed?

Find out what the raw output points to. Here, the nearby code and comment concern storage that a later engine step can release or reuse. Appending the object to a list would only keep a reference to that storage, and the contents behind a reference can change.
Trace when the consumer reads the saved result and when the producer can overwrite the buffer behind it. If those moments can overlap, the copy is what keeps the two lifetimes apart.

Before removing it, write a test that saves one output, forces the engine to reuse the buffer, and then reads the saved output again. Any replacement has to keep that earlier value intact, either by copying or through an ownership protocol you can prove.

questions.prompt: What is the best first route through the repository?
options: Start with an example and follow one request through to its results.
Read every file in directory order, so nothing is missed, before tracing a request.
Start from the most optimized kernels, since they dominate the benchmark results.
questions.why: Following one request ties every file you open to behavior you can observe, so the map you build stays connected.
questions.hint: Follow one request, not the directory tree.
option_feedback: Right: one traced request shows how the pieces cooperate, and each file answers part of a question you already have.
Reading in directory order covers files without showing how they connect, so the details rarely add up to a map.
Kernels matter for speed, but without the request loop you cannot tell when they run or what they receive.

questions.prompt: In schedule_mtp_varlen.py, two sequences share total_q = 4. A’s running products are 0.9, 0.5, 0.2 and B’s are 0.7, 0.6, 0.1. How many positions does each verify?
options: A verifies 3 and B verifies 1
A verifies 2 and B verifies 2
A verifies 1 and B verifies 3
questions.why: Each sequence gets one mandatory slot, leaving 4 − 2 = 2 extra. The two highest products overall are A’s 0.9 and B’s 0.7, so each sequence adds one position: 2 and 2.
questions.hint: Subtract one mandatory slot per sequence first, then rank all products together.
option_feedback: That gives A two extra slots, but A’s second product, 0.5, ranks below both of B’s first two products.
Right: the extra budget is 2, and the top two products, 0.9 and 0.7, belong to different sequences.
B would need its first two products to beat A’s 0.9, and 0.7 and 0.6 do not.

questions.prompt: An output is cloned just before the engine may reuse its buffers. What should you check before calling the clone waste?
options: Whether a saved result would change after the buffer is reused
Whether the optimizer state is updated during inference
Whether the clone makes the output tensor larger
questions.why: If the consumer reads after the producer has overwritten the buffer, removing the copy lets it read changed data.
questions.hint: Relate the copy to async reuse.
option_feedback: Right: the clone may be what keeps the saved result’s lifetime separate from the reused buffer’s.
Inference does not run an optimizer, so optimizer state cannot explain a copy in the generation loop.
A clone has the same shape and size as its source; the question is whether its values stay fixed.

transfer: Trace one request through DeepInfer in a few sentences. Name one property you would test at a specific boundary.
Traces entrypoint to scheduling to execution to sampling
Names request-owned state
Names an observable invariant

The example creates the model and calls generation. The entry point admits the requests, then repeatedly asks the engine to schedule and execute work. Model execution produces the values that sampling uses, and result handling updates each request and collects its outputs. Each request keeps its own state. At the output-collection boundary, I would test that an output saved earlier stays unchanged after a later step reuses the producer’s buffer.
LESSONS.takeaway: Build your map by following one request, then study one responsibility at a time.

activity.title: Trace one request and name the promise at one boundary.
activity.intro: Open the pinned entry point below. Start at generate, follow the loop that collects outputs, and find where an output is copied before it is kept. The task covers one small path through the engine.

fields.label: In your own words, what enters and leaves this path?

compare: Follow the actual function calls and the values they save. A function’s name alone does not tell you its responsibility.
One useful promise is that a result kept for the caller stays unchanged after the engine reuses temporary storage.
Use outputs you can tell apart, and read the first saved value again after a later engine step. Comparing shapes alone would miss a changed value.
activity.example: For the output-copy boundary, I would create an output containing token 7, let the collector save it, then reuse the producer’s storage for token 9. The saved first output should still contain 7. This checks one lifetime promise; it does not prove every engine path correct.

levels.1:
You can understand one path through a repository before you understand every file.

Opening a large engine repository can feel like walking into the middle of a conversation. There are kernels, worker processes, configuration flags, and several different objects that each represent a request. Reading the files in alphabetical order rarely shows how these pieces cooperate.

A better start is one concrete question: what happens when this example asks the model for a response? Follow that request from input to output, and let each function you meet answer a smaller part of the question.

Begin with the example’s inputs.

Open examples/offline_inference.py. Find where it chooses a model, sets how many devices take part, creates the engine and asks for outputs. Most of the options can wait. Write down what the example passes into generation and what it expects to get back.

Find the public entry point.

Next, open deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py. Its generation method admits requests and then runs a loop until they finish. Follow the call that adds a request, and then the loop that collects its outputs.

As you read, ask where each request’s identity comes from, which state belongs to it, and how its results come back in the right order. Those questions tie the code to the engine responsibilities you already know.

Then follow one execution step.

In deepinfer/engine/llm_engine.py, find the step method, the scheduling call, the asynchronous execution and the result handling. The scheduler picks the work, model execution performs it, and post-processing updates each request’s state. Trace that sequence once before you open any kernel.

Choose one detail to investigate.

In the entry point, output objects are cloned before the next step can reuse their underlying storage. A copy on a hot path looks like an easy saving. The nearby comment ties this one to storage a later step can reuse, which makes it a clue about data lifetime before it is a candidate for deletion.

You could instead follow sampling into sampler.py and separate ordinary token selection from the verification of draft tokens. Whichever detail you pick, find the inputs it receives and the outputs it owns.

Keep track of what kind of claim each line of your notes is: something you saw in the code, something the authors report, or something you inferred. The source links in this course pin a specific commit, so a colleague can open exactly the code you read.
levels.2:
From the caller to the engine.

LLM.generate in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py accepts text prompts or prompt_token_ids, plus one SamplingParams object or a list of them. For each prompt it calls _add_request, which deep-copies the sampling parameters so one request’s bookkeeping cannot leak into another’s, draws a string request ID from a counter, and, when given text, calls tokenizer.encode directly. No chat template is applied anywhere in this path; formatting is the caller’s job. The IDs become a one-dimensional np.int32 array.

LLMEngine.add_request wraps them in a Sequence. A request with a structured-output schema is not queued yet: its grammar compiles asynchronously, and a callback enqueues it once the compiled matcher is ready. Every other request goes straight to scheduler.add_sequence.

The loop and its lockstep condition.

_run_engine repeats one question: are there unfinished requests? has_unfinished_requests answers it with an all-reduce across the data-parallel group using MAX, so every rank keeps stepping until the last rank is done. Ranks have to step together because expert-parallel communication inside the model needs every participant, even a rank with nothing left to run.

Each step calls the C++ scheduler, which returns a list of SequenceMetadata and a SchedulerOutputs record. The record says whether this is a prompt step and which sequences were scheduled or finished, and it lists cache states and blocks to clone. A clone happens when a request forks from a shared prefix and must not write into blocks another request still reads. _execute_model_async_step then asks the workers to run execute_model_step and returns an array of uint64 handles to output objects.

Outputs arrive one step late and expire one step later.

With zero-overhead scheduling on, which is the default for normal engines, the CPU schedules step N+1 while the GPU is still running step N. The docstring of process_output states the consequence: the outputs handled during a step belong to the previous step. When no work remains, the loop calls flush_inflight_reqs once to collect the last step still in flight, and only then breaks.

The output handles point into a RequestOutputPool. The step docstring says they are released automatically at the next step, and the DeferredRelease class performs that release during the following pre_sampler_sync, overlapped with GPU work. That is why _run_engine calls RequestOutput.clone on every raw output before appending it to a list. Remove the clone and the list holds handles to pooled objects that a later step reuses. At the end, results are sorted by integer request ID. The default decode_sequence=True returns decoded strings; the examples pass False to keep per-token objects with log-probabilities and draft statistics.

A small kernel worth checking by hand.

schedule_mtp_varlen.py decides how many draft tokens each sequence verifies. Its inputs are each sequence’s confidence for its draft positions and a total query budget total_q. Phase 1 turns each sequence’s confidences into running products, the estimated chance that every draft up to that position is accepted, using 0 for a sequence with no previous step. Phase 2 ranks every (sequence, position) pair against all others. Each sequence gets one mandatory slot for the target model’s own token, plus one more for each of its positions that ranks inside the remaining total_q − num_seqs.

Take two sequences with three drafts each and total_q = 5, leaving 3 extra slots. Sequence A has confidences 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5, giving products 0.9, 0.72 and 0.36. Sequence B has 0.6, 0.9 and 0.9, giving 0.6, 0.54 and 0.486. The top three products are 0.9 and 0.72 from A and 0.6 from B, so A verifies 1 + 2 = 3 positions and B verifies 1 + 1 = 2. A running product of numbers at most 1 cannot increase, and ties go to the lower flat index, so a sequence’s selected positions always form a prefix of its draft.

A practical note: many comments in the repository are written in Chinese. A translation tool handles them well, and they often state the invariant the code relies on, as the DeferredRelease docstring does.
levels.3:
The tests are the best map of what the authors promise.

Function names tell you responsibilities. The tests under tests/models tell you which properties DeepSeek considered important enough to check on real hardware, and how strictly.

  • test_offline_inference.py compares decode perplexities against baselines in offline_decode_ppl.json, keyed by platform and workload, exactly and sample by sample. The examples README describes a separate script for refreshing those baselines once a numerical change has been confirmed as intended.
  • test_batch_invariant.py runs the same prompts batched and singly with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 and requires identical tokens and log-probabilities.
  • test_kl.py decodes long image-and-text prompts, folds the generated tokens back into the prompt, recomputes everything in one prefill, and bounds the KL divergence between the two sets of log-probabilities. For the listed case the bound is 0.
  • test_sampler.py checks that sampled tokens follow the intended distribution with a randomized probability integral transform and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, across greedy and several temperature and top-p settings.

These tests separate three kinds of claim: bit-for-bit reproducibility under a flag, equivalence between two execution paths, and statistical correctness of sampling. A change that touches one path should name which of the three it preserves.

Judge a candidate change against a lifetime contract.

The output clone in _run_engine is a good test case for reading judgment. A profiler shows a copy on every step, and the copy looks removable. The code makes a different promise: step returns pooled objects, and DeferredRelease frees them one step later so the caller can finish reading. Removing the clone safely means replacing that contract, for example by consuming outputs before the next step or by moving ownership of the pooled object explicitly to the caller. A test that saves one output, runs another step and reads the saved output again can tell the two designs apart. Comparing shapes cannot.

The same reasoning applies to the confidence scheduler. A useful contribution writes a plain reference for it in Python: running products, a global ranking with ties broken by flat index, and one mandatory slot per sequence. Then it compares the kernel against that reference over random confidences, fresh sequences, ties and budgets at both edges, from total_q equal to the number of sequences up to every position selected. The kernel’s correctness rests on two properties, that each sequence’s selection is a prefix of its draft and that the selected positions add up to total_q. Those are the properties to test.

Know the lineage, and where it stops.

The README says DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM, with ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM, and 21 files in the package carry a “Derived from vLLM” header. vLLM’s documentation helps you read class names like LLMEngine and SamplingParams. The scheduler has moved to C++, the asynchronous scheduling follows the overlap design that the Q&A credits to SGLang and NanoFlow, and the release supports one model family on two kinds of accelerator. Assume nothing from vLLM without checking the pinned file.

A change can also be the wrong size for this repository. The README lists what the release leaves out: the cache storage system, disaggregated serving and load balancing. A pull request adding an online server or a new model architecture is a design question for the maintainers before it is a patch; CONTRIBUTING.md covers formatting and test conventions, and says nothing about scope. A corrected benchmark, a reference test for an existing kernel or a fixed lifetime bug can be judged on its evidence alone.

Some invariants are still unchecked by any test you can run without the target hardware. Every test above needs SM100 GPUs or Ascend NPUs and the full checkpoint. A CPU-runnable reference for small kernels such as the confidence scheduler would let more people check changes, and the absence of one is a gap worth knowing about when you read a claim that the kernel is correct.

LESSONS.title: Your fine-tuned model is more than a weights file
LESSONS.goal: Know which files and settings you need to reproduce the model you fine-tuned.
LESSONS.recall: Why can the wrong tokenizer make correct weights behave incorrectly?
LESSONS.predict: If two checkpoints share an architecture name, can you apply the same LoRA adapter to either base revision?
example: An adapter trained on base revision R1 loads on R2 without a shape error. Have you established that it is the model you trained?

A clean load shows that some structural expectations were met. It does not show that R2 contains the base values the adapter was trained to modify, because matching dimensions leave that question open.
Recover the intended base revision and the adapter configuration from the training record. Keep the tokenizer, the custom prompt format and the stop settings consistent with training too.

Load that exact combination in a reference implementation. Feed a deployment path the same tokenized inputs and compare, then check the behavior you want on a separate evaluation set. That establishes far more than a successful load.

questions.prompt: A LoRA adapter is usually…
options: A replacement tokenizer trained for the new task
A learned update that needs a compatible base model
A complete copy of the fine-tuned weights
questions.why: The adapter modifies selected base operations and usually omits the base weights, so it can only run on top of a compatible base.
questions.hint: Where are the original large matrices?
option_feedback: LoRA trains changes to weight matrices; the tokenizer comes from the base model and stays the same.
Right: the adapter stores a small update, and the large base matrices have to come from the matching base model.
A merged checkpoint is a full copy, but a saved LoRA adapter usually holds only the low-rank update.

questions.prompt: An adapter was trained with r = 16, lora_alpha = 32 and use_rslora on. A loader ignores the rsLoRA flag. What happens?
options: Loading fails with a shape error, because rsLoRA adapters store larger matrices
The update is applied at scale 2 instead of 8, a quarter of its trained size, with no error
Nothing changes, because the scale is stored in the weights rather than in the configuration
questions.why: Ordinary LoRA scales by lora_alpha / r = 32 / 16 = 2, while rsLoRA scales by lora_alpha / √r = 32 / 4 = 8. The matrices are identical, so only the configuration says which scale is right.
questions.hint: Compute lora_alpha / r and lora_alpha / √r.
option_feedback: rsLoRA changes only the scaling factor; A and B have the same shapes as in ordinary LoRA, so nothing fails to load.
Right: dropping the flag swaps √r for r in the denominator, shrinking the update by a factor of 4 while every shape still matches.
The saved A and B matrices carry no scale; the loader computes it from lora_alpha, r and the variant flag in the configuration.

levels.1:
A weights file is only part of the model you trained.

Suppose you fine-tune a base model and want to run the result in an inference engine. It is tempting to think a weights file finishes the job. The engine also needs to know what those numbers mean, and how inputs were represented while the model learned them.

First, the engine must support the model’s architecture, the arrangement of layers and calculations that its configuration describes. Fine-tuning changes the learned numbers inside that arrangement and leaves the arrangement itself alone. An engine that cannot execute the base model cannot execute your tuned version either.

An adapter may contain only the change.

With LoRA, a common fine-tuning method, you train a compact update attached to selected matrices of the base model. The saved adapter usually leaves out the base weights themselves. To run it you need the compatible base, the adapter’s configuration and its learned values.

Two revisions of a base model can share every dimension and still hold different learned numbers. An adapter trained on one may load onto the other without a shape error, and the clean load says nothing about whether it now computes what you trained.

The text format is part of what the model learned.

A tokenizer assigns IDs to pieces of text and to special markers. A chat template arranges messages and roles into the token sequence a chat-trained model expects to see. A completion model may instead expect whatever custom format you used during training.

Change any of these and behavior can shift while every weight loads cleanly. Keep the intended tokenizer, input format and stop-token rules with the model files.

Record enough to rebuild the same computation.

An artifact manifest is a short record of the pieces you used: the exact base revision, the adapter or merged weights, the model configuration, the tokenizer and format, the numerical precision and the relevant library versions. A name like “latest base” points somewhere new each time the base is updated, so record an immutable revision.

You can serve an adapter next to its supported base, or, where the tooling allows, merge its update into a full set of weights. Each route needs its own checks, especially once reduced precision or quantization is involved.

Before optimizing anything, load the intended combination in a reference implementation and save a few fixed inputs with their expected scores or task results. When an engine later appears to run the model, those saved cases give you something concrete to compare against.
levels.2:
What a LoRA adapter stores, in numbers.

For a frozen weight matrix W with d_out rows and d_in columns, LoRA learns two thin matrices: B with d_out rows and r columns, and A with r rows and d_in columns. The adapted weight is W′ = W + s·BA, where r is the rank and s is a scaling factor. B starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model.

The savings come from r being small. A 4,096 × 4,096 projection has 16,777,216 entries, 32 MiB in BF16 at 2 bytes each. At r = 16 the adapter for that matrix has 16 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 131,072 entries, 256 KiB, about 0.8% of the original. The base matrix is absent from the adapter file, which is why the adapter is useless without the exact base it was trained against.

The configuration decides what the numbers mean.

A PEFT adapter directory usually holds adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors. The configuration records the base model’s name, the rank r, lora_alpha, the target_modules the update attaches to, and variant flags. Ordinary LoRA uses s = lora_alpha / r. With use_rslora, the rank-stabilized variant, s = lora_alpha / √r.

A loader that ignores a flag fails silently. Take r = 16 and lora_alpha = 32. Ordinary scaling gives s = 2 and rank-stabilized scaling gives s = 8. A loader that drops the rsLoRA flag applies a quarter of the trained update, and every shape still matches. The tensor names inside the safetensors file encode module paths, so a base with renamed modules fails loudly. A base with the same names but a different revision loads cleanly with different values underneath.

Merged and unmerged routes compute the same thing differently.

For an input row x, the unmerged route computes xWᵀ + s·(xAᵀ)Bᵀ, which adds about r × (d_in + d_out) multiply-adds per token for each adapted matrix. The merged route folds s·BA into W once and then costs nothing extra, but the result is a full checkpoint tied to one adapter. Unmerged serving lets one copy of the base serve several adapters. In exact arithmetic the two routes agree; in BF16 they round at different points, so their outputs can differ in the last digits.

Text becomes IDs through two separate artifacts.

The tokenizer maps strings to IDs. A chat template, stored for Hugging Face models as a Jinja template in tokenizer_config.json, decides which strings the tokenizer sees. apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True) appends the header that tells a chat model its turn has begun; leave it off and the model sees a different sequence. The Transformers documentation also warns that templated text already contains its special tokens, so tokenizing it again with add_special_tokens=True can duplicate a beginning-of-sequence token.

What DeepInfer does with each artifact.

The LLM constructor in deepinfer/entrypoints/llm.py takes model, tokenizer, revision and tokenizer_revision, so a pinned commit can be passed for both. _add_request calls tokenizer.encode on raw text and applies no template; the offline examples use plain few-shot completion prompts. DeepSeek’s chat formatting lives in a separate component, DeepSeek Recipe, which the Q&A describes as converting API requests into token sequences. It also encodes strings such as <｜User｜> that appear inside user text as ordinary tokens, so pasted text cannot inject control tokens.

The release supports one model family and has no adapter loader. A search of the package for LoRA finds only kv_lora_rank, which is the compressed attention dimension of DeepSeek’s multi-head latent attention, a low-rank projection built into the architecture. It has nothing to do with fine-tuning adapters, and the name is easy to misread.

A sensible check order follows from the pipeline: confirm the configuration and module names, then token IDs for fixed strings, then logits on fixed IDs, then task behavior.
levels.3:
Where LoRA came from, and what it assumes.

Edward Hu and colleagues introduced LoRA in 2021, reporting that low-rank updates to the attention projections matched full fine-tuning on several benchmarks while training far fewer parameters. The assumption that matters for deployment is quieter: the update is defined relative to one specific frozen base. QLoRA, by Tim Dettmers and colleagues (2023), trained adapters on a base stored in 4-bit NF4 format. The adapter then learned to correct a quantized base, and serving it on a BF16 copy of that base, or merging it into dequantized weights, is a different computation from the one training saw. Whether the difference matters for a given model is an empirical question. Measure it on held-out data before choosing a serving route.

Serving many adapters changes the system design.

Once adapters stay unmerged, a single base can serve many of them. S-LoRA, by Ying Sheng and colleagues (2023), stored adapter weights in a paged pool alongside the attention cache and batched requests for different adapters together. Punica, by Lequn Chen and colleagues (2023), wrote a kernel for that mixed batch, in which each request multiplies by its own low-rank pair. vLLM’s adapter serving is in this tradition. The trade is real: an unmerged batch pays the extra low-rank work and kernel complexity, and a merged checkpoint pays a full copy of the weights per adapter.

Shared serving makes adapter identity part of the cache key. An adapter attached to the key and value projections changes the attention cache for every token it touches. A prefix cache keyed on token IDs alone would hand keys and values computed under adapter A to a request running adapter B, producing a mixture of the two models that no one trained. vLLM’s prefix-caching design adds LoRA IDs, along with image hashes and an optional cache salt, to the hash of each block. A custom cache needs the same care.

Judging a numerical difference.

Suppose merged and unmerged routes give BF16 logits that differ slightly. BF16 keeps 8 significant bits, so each rounding step can introduce a relative error of up to about 2⁻⁸, roughly 0.4%. A difference of that order, scattered without a pattern across positions, fits rounding. A wrong scaling factor or a skipped target module looks different: a systematic shift that grows with the size of the adapter’s contribution, and that moves task scores.

The evidence that separates the two is a third computation. Run both routes in FP32 on the same IDs. If they agree closely there, and each BF16 route sits near its FP32 counterpart, the BF16 gap is rounding. Then confirm on a held-out task that the adapted model still differs from the base where training intended. Declare the tolerance before looking at the result, and choose it from a known source of benign variation, such as the gap between two orderings in a reference implementation.

Provenance is still an open practice.

Hugging Face Hub revisions are git commits, and safetensors files can be hashed, so the weights themselves are easy to pin. The rest of the computation has no standard record. Template, stop rules, scaling variant, quantization method and engine version are scattered across configuration files, model cards and training scripts. A manifest worth keeping covers them all:

  • Base model ID and immutable revision, plus a hash of its configuration
  • Tokenizer revision, template text and stop tokens
  • Adapter rank, alpha, scaling variant and target modules
  • Precision and quantization method, during training and at serving time
  • Library and engine versions and context settings
  • Fixed token-ID fixtures and the revision of the evaluation set

Open questions remain. No established method says when an adapter trained on one base revision remains valid on the next. Equivalence across quantization formats is usually argued from task scores, which miss rare behaviors. And a fine-tuned completion model gains nothing from a chat template invented after training; the format it learned is the one it should receive.

The second input adds an entry at position 1. Starting the read at 0 keeps both entries. Attention splits its weight between the two saved values, and the cached scores still agree with the reference.

With two saved positions, starting at 1 leaves position 0 out of both slices. Equal slice lengths only show that the keys and values are still paired; they say nothing about whether the intended history is present. activity.title: Repair the highlighted cache read.
activity.intro: The cache now has positions 0 and 1. Change the highlighted start value, predict which entries attention will receive, and run the selected branch of the actual CPU engine.

levels.1:
A cache lets the engine skip recomputing earlier tokens, but attention still has to read every piece of history it needs. Below, you will trace two token positions through the code above, then repair a one-line change that quietly drops part of that history.

Read the slice before running the model.

Python counts positions from zero. With two saved entries, [0:] selects positions 0 and 1, and [1:] selects only position 1. The colon means “from here to the end.” The stored arrays keep their full size; the slice decides which entries the calculation receives.

What is actually stored?

Each saved entry holds a key and a value, two vectors of numbers computed from a token and its position. The query, named q in the code, comes from the current token. Attention compares the query with each visible key and uses the resulting weights to mix the matching values.

Leave an entry out of the read and its contribution to that mixture disappears. The rest of the model then works from a different mixture and produces different next-token scores. The key and value slices can still have equal lengths while the calculation is wrong.

Why does starting at position 1 change the scores?

That is the question to answer once the second input arrives. In “See an example,” watch the actual entries and attention weights at each position. In “Try it,” change the highlighted value, predict which entries remain, and run your version. Then explain why your repair is justified.

The small model uses random weights and numbered tokens, so its output will never read as fluent language. It is there to make each step of the calculation visible.
levels.2:
The tiny engine’s shapes.

tiny_engine.py builds one transformer block with random weights: width 12, a vocabulary of 16 token IDs, one attention head, learned position vectors, a residual connection and a small tanh MLP. input_vector adds a token’s 12-number embedding to its position’s 12-number vector. Three 12 × 12 matrices turn that input into a query, a key and a value. After n tokens the cache holds n keys and n values, each a list of 12 numbers.

attention_weights scores each visible key against the query as a dot product divided by √12, then applies softmax, giving one weight per visible position that sums to 1. attention returns the weighted sum of the visible values, again 12 numbers. finish_block applies the output projection, the residual, a 24-wide hidden layer and the projection back. output_logits multiplies by a 16 × 12 head, producing 16 next-token scores.

Two paths to the same scores.

full_logits is the reference. For a prefix of length n it recomputes the query, key and value at every position and lets position i attend to positions 0 through i. Producing the scores for each new token this way repeats all earlier work, so total work over a generation grows roughly with the square of its length. cached_step computes the query, key and value for the new token only, appends the key and value to the cache, and attends over the stored lists.

Both paths perform the same scalar operations on the same numbers in the same order, so the lab can use a tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰. A vectorized port would sum in a different order, and its tolerance would have to be chosen from the size of double-precision rounding over that many additions.

Where the broken read first shows up.

With broken_offset on, the read starts at 1 once the cache holds more than one entry. The lesson’s prompt is token IDs 1, 4, 2, 8. At prefix length 1 the cache has one entry, the condition is false and the scores match exactly. At prefix length 2 the reference splits attention between positions 0 and 1, while the broken read sees only position 1 and gives it weight 1.0. The largest score difference is about 0.165. At lengths 3 and 4 position 0 stays missing, and the differences are about 0.097 and 0.059. Those smaller numbers do not mean the bug is fading. Each new entry dilutes the missing one’s share of attention, and a smaller error is still the wrong computation.

Greedy text is a weaker signal. The highest-scoring token can survive a 0.165 shift in some scores, so a broken cache can produce the right next token for a while. Comparing all 16 scores at every position catches the error at the first prefix where it exists.

What the reference checks cover.

The “Try it” panel runs reference_checks, which reports 218 comparisons. For three seeds and prompt lengths 1, 2, 7, 16 and 33, it compares cached and full-prefix scores after every position, which is 177 comparisons. It also compares 15 six-token greedy continuations. It interleaves two requests with separate caches and compares each to its own reference, 24 comparisons that would catch a shared-cache leak. It checks one constructed rank-2 update to the output head, explicit against merged into the weights. Finally it confirms that a model with a maximum context of 2 rejects a third token without appending to the cache. That update is a hand-built example, and the tiny engine loads no trained adapters.

For a scheduler extension, the same pattern holds: compare each request against its own independent generation, including requests that finish early and a new request that takes over a freed slot.
levels.3:
The same oracle runs in DeepInfer’s test suite.

tests/models/test_kl.py is the production version of this lab. It builds image-and-text prompts of 16,384 tokens and decodes 1,024 tokens per prompt with temperature 0.5 and top-p 0.95. The tokens are forced to a fixed golden sequence, so the run’s path does not depend on sampling. It then appends the generated tokens to the prompt and runs the whole sequence again as one prefill, asking for the log-probability of every prompt token. Two assertions follow. The prompt log-probabilities must be identical across the two runs, and the KL divergence between decode-time and prefill-time log-probabilities must not exceed max_kl, which is 0 for the case in the file. The run has speculative drafting at length 5, context parallelism, expert parallelism over 8 GPUs and DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1.

The bound of zero depends on the flag. Without batch invariance, a reduction can be split differently depending on how many tokens share the batch, and a decode step and a long prefill sum the same numbers in different orders. Horace He and colleagues at Thinking Machines Lab described this source of nondeterminism in 2025 and showed kernels that remove it. DeepInfer’s README offers batch-invariant inference on NVIDIA hardware only. Where invariance is unavailable, a nonzero tolerance is unavoidable. deepinfer.testing.cal_diff reports cosine difference, root-mean-square error, the largest single difference and KL divergence, which gives four ways to see the size and shape of a disagreement.

Two implementations can share a bug.

Comparing two implementations of one specification is differential testing, a name William McKeeman gave the practice in 1998. Its weakness shows in the tiny engine. full_logits and cached_step call the same input_vector, attention and finish_block. A wrong scaling factor inside attention would appear in both and pass every comparison. The cache-offset bug is caught because it lives in the one line the paths do not share.

Independent checks fill that gap. A hand-computed case with two positions and tiny integer weights checks the arithmetic directly. Invariants catch whole classes of error: attention weights sum to 1, and the scores for a prefix do not depend on tokens after it. Metamorphic checks change something that should not matter, such as which other request shares the batch, and require the output to stay the same. The lab’s interleaved-request check is one.

Some correctness claims are distributional.

Sampling cannot be checked by comparing one output, since a correct sampler produces different tokens on different runs. tests/models/test_sampler.py instead generates 128 trajectories per configuration and applies a randomized probability integral transform: if each token was drawn from the distribution the engine reports, the transformed values are uniform between 0 and 1. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test then checks uniformity. Speculative decoding, as Yaniv Leviathan and colleagues defined it in 2023, promises the same output distribution as the target model, which is a claim of this kind. A logit comparison cannot establish it.

Extend one mechanism at a time.

  • Add an explicit maximum-context policy, reject or truncate, and test it. Silently changing what attention sees changes behavior.
  • Add continuous admission with two active slots. Keep the caches separate and compare every request with its independent generation, including early finishes and slot reuse.
  • Port the arithmetic to NumPy or PyTorch, keep the scalar version as the oracle, and choose a tolerance from the change in summation order.
  • Then add paged storage, testing lengths of one page minus one, exactly one page and one page plus one, along with page reuse.

The oracle has to stay cheaper than the system it checks. DeepInfer’s KL test needs eight GPUs and the full checkpoint. The tiny engine runs in milliseconds on a laptop, and that is why it can be run after every change.
