levels.1:
Make the first deployment a controlled comparison.

You want two things from a first deployment. It should run the model you actually trained, and it should run that model efficiently. Settle the first before the second justifies any change. If you change both at once and the output differs, you cannot tell whether the model files, the input format, the numerical format or the engine caused it.

Choose an engine by the calculations it supports.

Start from the exact architecture and configuration of your base model. Check that the engine supports that architecture, the adapter path you use and the numerical format you plan to serve. vLLM’s supported-models page is one place to look this up.

DeepInfer is the advanced case study in this course, and its design is built around DeepSeek’s own models. It makes no promise to run every model fine-tuned from every base. A compatible general-purpose engine is often the more practical first home for your model.

Save a small set of fixed inputs.

Use the correct tokenizer and the training-time format to produce prompt IDs. Record the stop rules and generation settings, and keep all of it fixed whenever you compare the reference with the engine.

Fixed IDs prevent a common confusion. Two systems can show the same question on screen and still run different token sequences, because each formatted it differently.

Check the model before putting an API around it.

Load the intended base plus adapter, or the intended merged checkpoint, in a direct reference implementation. Save numerical predictions where you can, and score examples from a held-out set. A held-out set contains cases you kept out of training, so it shows how the model behaves beyond the examples it was fitted to.

Then run the compatible engine on the same inputs. Compare next-token probabilities where the engine exposes them, greedy outputs under controlled settings, and the task results you care about. When only the weaker comparisons are available, say so in your notes.

Add complexity one change at a time.

Once offline generation matches, add a local endpoint and then concurrent requests. Test limits, cancellation, a range of input lengths and reloading. Evaluate quantization as its own experiment, so that any change in quality has one identifiable cause.

An HTTP 200 response tells you the endpoint answered. On its own it cannot show that your adapter was active or that the model still behaves as it did in the reference. Keep the artifact identities and reference comparisons next to the service measurements.
levels.2:
Build the comparison table before the server.

Give the table four rows: the base model in a reference implementation, the adapted model in that reference, the adapted model in the engine, and optionally a quantized engine run. A difference between the first two rows is what fine-tuning changed. A difference between the second and third is execution. A difference between the third and fourth is numerical representation. Each comparison changes one thing.

Teacher-forced log-probabilities are the strongest comparison.

Take a fixed prompt and a fixed continuation, for example the reference model’s greedy output. Feed prompt plus continuation to each system as one input and read the log-probability each assigns to every token. Every position then sees identical inputs, so one disagreement cannot cascade into different later text. In vLLM the prompt_logprobs field of SamplingParams returns these values for the prompt tokens. DeepInfer’s own tests follow the same pattern: test_kl.py passes golden_token_ids to force a continuation and prompt_logprobs=True to read the recomputed values. Report the largest and mean absolute difference per token, and note where the top-ranked token changes.

When an engine exposes no log-probabilities, compare greedy continuations under fixed settings and record the first position where they diverge. A divergence at a near-tie between two tokens is weak evidence of a bug; one at a confident position is strong evidence. Task scores on held-out data come last. They answer whether the model still does its job, which neither of the other comparisons can settle.

Prove the adapter is active.

vLLM serves adapters when started with --enable-lora and a --lora-modules entry mapping a name to an adapter path. A request then selects the adapter by putting that name in its model field, and the response echoes the name back. The echo shows the name was accepted. Whether the adapter’s numbers were applied is a separate fact. Pick held-out prompts where the base and adapted references differ clearly, and check that the engine matches the adapted row. If it matches the base row, the update never took effect.

Size memory before choosing hardware.

Weights take parameters × bytes per parameter. The attention cache per token takes 2 (one key, one value) × layers × key-value heads × head dimension × bytes. For a model shaped like Llama 3 8B, with 32 layers, 8 key-value heads and head dimension 128 in BF16, that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token. The 8 billion weights take about 16 GB.

On an 80 GB GPU with the common 0.9 memory-utilization setting, which is also the default in DeepInfer’s LLM, the engine reserves 72 GB. Subtract 16 GB of weights and a few GB of activations and workspace, and roughly 54 GB remains for cache: about 412,000 tokens, or about 50 requests holding 8,192 tokens each. Quantizing the weights frees memory for cache. Quantizing the cache halves its per-token cost in an 8-bit format. Each is a separate row in the table.

Where DeepInfer fits.

The release supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs and documents no adapter path. Its low-precision formats were chosen with that model: the Q&A lists FP4 variants for the main cache, the indexer cache and the routed expert weights. For most fine-tuned models DeepInfer is reading material, and a general engine with documented support for the architecture is where the first deployment runs.

Service checks come after the table matches.

Then add the endpoint and test it under mixed prompt lengths, concurrent requests, cancellation mid-stream, requests at the context limit, and a restart or reload. After a reload, run the fixed fixtures again and compare them with the saved rows.

LESSONS.title: Judge a performance claim and test one change
LESSONS.goal: Explain whether an engine change helped, using evidence another person can reproduce.
LESSONS.recall: Which correctness promise did your last optimization actually make?
LESSONS.predict: A chart says 2× faster. What would you need to know to decide whether that helps your workload?
example: Configuration A produces 2,000 tokens/s with p99 token gaps of 180 ms. B produces 1,600 tokens/s with p99 gaps of 60 ms. Your limit is 80 ms. Which qualifies?
Apply the requirement before you look at throughput. A’s p99 gap of 180 milliseconds exceeds the 80-millisecond limit. B’s 60 milliseconds is within it.

Of these two measured configurations, only B meets the latency requirement, even though its aggregate throughput is 400 tokens/s lower. That conclusion assumes their quality checks and measurement boundaries are comparable.

Judging cost efficiency, or carrying the result to another workload, needs more information: hardware cost, workload details and the other relevant measurements. Two rows of measurements are not a universal ranking.

questions.prompt: The authors’ benchmark shows a 2× speedup. Can you expect the same speedup for your deployment?
options: Yes, because the engine code is the same
No; the workload and configuration limit what the result shows
Yes, as long as your cluster is at least as large as theirs
questions.why: A benchmark is evidence about the conditions it measured. Your request lengths, arrivals, precision and cache state may differ.
questions.hint: What variables were held fixed?
option_feedback: The same code can behave very differently under other request lengths, batch sizes or cache states.
Right: the speedup belongs to the measured workload and configuration until you reproduce it under yours.
Hardware is only one condition; a different workload on equal hardware can still lose the gain.

questions.prompt: A: 2,000 tok/s, p99 ITL 180 ms. B: 1,600 tok/s, p99 60 ms. Limit 80 ms. Choose…
options: A, because its throughput is higher
B, among these measured configurations
Either, since p99 describes only the slowest 1% of gaps
questions.why: A’s 180 ms p99 gap breaks the 80 ms limit and B’s 60 ms meets it, so B is the only configuration that qualifies.
questions.hint: Filter by the actual requirement before maximizing throughput.
option_feedback: Higher throughput counts only among configurations that already meet the latency requirement, and A misses it.
Right: filter by the 80 ms requirement first, and B is the only one left.
The requirement is stated as a p99 limit, so the slowest 1% of gaps is exactly what it constrains.

questions.prompt: A write-up says confidence-scheduled verification raised throughput 5% and cites DeepSeek’s Q&A. What is the most important thing to check before relying on it?
options: The concurrency it applies at, since the Q&A’s estimates run from −1.5% at 16 sequences per rank to +11% at 96
Whether the 5% was measured with the profiler on, since profiling only adds noise and the mean is unaffected
Nothing further, since the gain came from the engine’s authors on production hardware
questions.why: The Q&A’s figures are estimates whose sign and size depend on concurrency per rank. A 5% gain belongs to one operating point, and yours may sit elsewhere on the curve.
questions.hint: Did the Q&A report one number or a curve?
option_feedback: Right: the gain changes sign at low concurrency, so the operating point decides whether the claim applies to you.
Profiling does matter, but it inflates step times systematically rather than adding zero-mean noise, and the Q&A figures came from benchmark data in any case.
Author-reported figures are evidence about the authors' workload; the table itself shows the result depends on load.

transfer: Choose one DeepInfer idea and explain whether you would adopt it for your own model. What evidence would you need?
Names saved resource and new cost
States architectural and hardware assumptions
Defines a correctness oracle and matched benchmark

For confidence-based draft scheduling, I would first check that my model and engine support the drafting and verification path it needs. I would measure the acceptance rate and the cost of verification under my target request load. I would keep the intended sampling behavior, confirmed by reference checks, and compare useful throughput at matched latency and quality targets. I would adopt the mechanism only if those measurements show a worthwhile gain for that workload.
LESSONS.takeaway: A useful speed claim names its baseline, its workload, its correctness promise and what the measurement includes.

activity.title: Make one change and decide what the evidence supports.
activity.intro: Use your own model experiment if you have one. Until then, write a proposed experiment and label every unmeasured result “not measured.” Choose one mechanism from the course; you can start applying it without a separate final project.

fields.label: What workload and user requirement will you keep fixed?
fields.placeholder: Prompt/output lengths, request arrivals, concurrency, cache state, hardware, numerical format, quality requirement, and a latency target.

fields.label: What one change will you try, and why?
fields.placeholder: The trace or other evidence suggests… I will change… I expect this tradeoff…

fields.label: What did the matched comparison actually show?
fields.placeholder: Correctness checks and tolerance, before/after timing and useful throughput, memory, task quality, and limits. Write “not measured” for missing evidence.

fields.label: Would you keep the change, and where might it fail?
fields.placeholder: Adopt, reject, or investigate further because… The result applies to… It does not establish…

compare: State exactly which model files, engine revision, hardware, inputs, numeric format, and cache conditions ran.
Use observed evidence to name a limiting resource. A plausible explanation alone is a hypothesis.
Change one mechanism, repeat the correctness checks, and rerun the same workload. Explain any remaining differences between configurations.
Keep latency and task quality requirements visible. A larger combined output rate does not establish lower user waiting time or equal cost.
A plan is useful before you have hardware, but it is still a plan. A decision about a measured gain needs the actual results and their limits.
activity.example: If a trace suggests repeated weight reads dominate my workload, I might test a different batch policy while keeping the model, hardware, inputs, numerical format, and cache state fixed. I would rerun reference checks and compare user waiting times, useful output rate, memory, and task quality under the same arrival pattern. I would keep the change only if the relevant requirement improves without an unacceptable regression. Before collecting those measurements, I would record this as a proposed experiment.

levels.1:
Start by asking what a benchmark compared.

Imagine a benchmark that reports twice as many tokens per second. You would like the same gain for your fine-tuned model. Before chasing it, find out what was compared and which conditions produced the result.

The GPU count, numerical format, request lengths, batch size and cache state can each move that number. When several of them changed together, the chart cannot tell you which one produced the gain.

Describe the workload as well as the model.

Record how long prompts and outputs are, how requests arrive, how many run at once and whether their prefixes are already cached. These conditions decide what kind of work the engine actually does.

A configuration that does well on many short requests can struggle with a few long-context ones. Running the same model does not make two workloads equivalent.

Keep quality and latency requirements in the comparison.

If users need an answer that streams smoothly, total throughput is not enough. Measure the wait before the first token, the gaps between later tokens and the slow tail of requests, and state which percentile has to meet your target.

Keep the correctness promise in view as well. An approximation that lowers task quality is a different trade from an exact rewrite that removes redundant work, and a headline speedup should say which one it is.

Make the result reproducible.

Save the exact model and adapter identities, code revision, hardware, library versions, precision settings, workload, warmup procedure and measurement commands. Another engineer should be able to tell what ran and what the numbers include.

A disappointing result can tempt you to try a different workload. If you do, label it as a new experiment. Finding that an optimization helps one case and hurts another is a useful result in its own right.

Put it together for your own model.

Use the notes and checks you have built so far to choose one justified code or configuration change for a supported deployment of your fine-tuned model. Show the reference comparison, the evidence for the bottleneck, the change itself and the repeated benchmark, and explain both the gain and its limits.

The same record works for the next model or engine you meet. When that one behaves differently, you will already know which conditions to compare first.
levels.2:
Define each number with its denominator.

Time to first token (TTFT) runs from a request’s arrival to its first output token, so it includes queueing and prefill. Inter-token latency (ITL) is the gap between successive tokens of one request. A percentile needs a population: the p99 of 10,000 pooled token gaps is set by the worst 100 gaps, which may all come from a few long requests, while the p99 of per-request mean gaps describes the slowest 1% of users. Say which one a target refers to.

Throughput needs a unit and a scope. Tokens per second per GPU, input or output tokens, all requests or only those that met their latency targets: each choice gives a different number from the same run.

How DeepInfer’s benchmark measures.

examples/benchmark.py, documented in the examples README, separates prefill from decode and measures each at steady state. Prefill throughput in tokens per second per GPU skips 5 warmup chunks and divides the tokens of 10 steady intervals by their duration and the number of devices. Decode speed, avg_SPS, is steps per second over 60 clean intervals, after 50 warmup steps and 60 logged steps. Intervals that collide with the periodic flush of expert-load statistics are dropped.

Decode throughput is then computed as avg_SPS × decode_num_requests × (1 + nextn) / cp. The README calls this full-acceptance accounting: each request is credited with 1 + nextn tokens per step, 6 at the default draft length of 5, whatever fraction of drafts the target model actually accepted. It is an upper bound. The plotting script sweep/plot_pareto.py rescales both axes by τ = 1 + nextn × a for an assumed acceptance a. At a = 0.75 and nextn = 5, τ = 4.75, so the full-acceptance figure is 6 / 4.75 ≈ 1.26 times the rescaled one. The script refuses to rescale runs with confidence-scheduled verification on, since their step counts already reflect acceptance.

The README also records two measurement hazards. With profiling on, step times inside the trace can be inflated by nearly 50% at batch size 1, so traces are for seeing which kernels run, never for computing speed. After the profiler exits, a residual slowdown of about 7 to 11% remains, so the profiler runs at the very end. The prefill plot uses measured step times, because dividing batch size by throughput assumes every step was full.

Run a matched comparison.

Hold fixed the model and adapter revisions, code revision, hardware and topology, library versions, numeric formats, the distributions of prompt and output lengths, the arrival process, warmup, cache state and sample count. Change one mechanism. Record failures, p50, p95 and p99 TTFT and ITL, useful throughput, peak memory and task score with its tolerance. If perfect matching is impossible, list the remaining differences and narrow the conclusion to what the data supports.

Compare configurations at a matched requirement: filter to those that meet the latency and quality targets, then rank the survivors by throughput or cost. Cost needs real prices and comparable useful work; a count of GPUs is not a cost.

A sequence that keeps causes separable: establish correctness, collect a trace, name the limiting resource, change one thing, recheck correctness, rerun the same workload.
levels.3:
A gain belongs to an operating point.

DeepSeek’s Q&A reports the effect of confidence-scheduled, variable-length verification against always verifying 5 drafts, on EP64/DP64 benchmark data. The average number of drafts verified per step falls from 5.00 to between 3.2 and 4.4, and the average accepted length barely moves, 3.29 against 3.20. The estimated throughput change depends on load: −1.5% at 16 concurrent sequences per rank, +1.6% at 32, +5.4% at 60 and +11.0% at 96. The headline, +4 to 7% at the production point of about 60 sequences per rank, is one region of that curve, and the figures are estimates computed from benchmark data. At low concurrency, where verification is cheap relative to the step, skipping drafts saves little and loses some accepted tokens. At high concurrency verification competes for compute, and dropping unlikely drafts pays.

The README’s charts follow the same discipline. They plot throughput against latency as Pareto curves, for prefill on 4 SM100 GPUs and for decode on 64, each within one scale-up domain. A single speedup figure answers less than the curve. A change that moves the curve outward helps everywhere; one that only extends it reaches a new operating point that your product may never use.

The same word can mean different quantities.

“75% acceptance” is ambiguous. DeepInfer’s plotting script treats it as the fraction of drafted tokens accepted, giving 1 + 5 × 0.75 = 4.75 tokens per step. Yaniv Leviathan and colleagues (2023) model acceptance as a per-position probability α, independent across positions, where one rejection discards the rest of the draft. With γ drafts the expected tokens per step are (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α). At α = 0.75 and γ = 5 that is (1 − 0.178) / 0.25 ≈ 3.29. The same phrase yields 4.75 or 3.29 depending on the model behind it, a gap of about 44%. A claim that depends on acceptance should state the definition and measure acceptance on the target workload.

How load is generated changes the latency you see.

A closed-loop benchmark keeps a fixed number of requests in flight and sends a new one only when another finishes. When the server stalls, the generator stops sending, and the requests that would have arrived during the stall never record their wait. Gil Tene named this coordinated omission. An open-loop generator draws arrival times independently of the server, for example from a Poisson process, and exposes queueing. MLPerf Inference, described by Vijay Janapa Reddi and colleagues (2020), separates these regimes into scenarios: Offline, where all queries are available at once and throughput is the metric, and Server, where queries arrive by a Poisson process and must meet a latency bound. DistServe’s goodput applies the same idea to the two latency targets of a language-model service.

Evidence a reviewer can rerun.

DeepInfer’s sweep script prints the git commit before each sweep, gives each point its own process and port, disables profiling for every measured point, and refuses to plot points whose model, expert-parallel size, context length, draft length or redundant-expert count disagree. Those are design choices worth copying: the record of what ran is produced by the same command that produced the numbers.

A negative result is part of that record. If a longer draft helps one user but lowers useful throughput at your target concurrency, the trade and the workload where it flips are the finding. Pick one DeepInfer mechanism, such as overlap scheduling, expert replication, the verification budget or bounded replay. State the resource it saves, the dependency it adds and the operating point where you expect it to help, then measure on your workload before adopting it.

Open problems remain. Published inference results rarely report arrival processes or the distribution of prompt lengths, cost per useful token is seldom given with prices attached, and equivalence claims for approximate mechanisms are often argued from averages that hide rare failures.

GLOSSARY.Activation: An intermediate numerical value produced while executing the model.
GLOSSARY.Adapter: A learned modification attached to compatible base weights; LoRA is one family.
GLOSSARY.Autoregressive: Each next-token prediction conditions on earlier tokens.
GLOSSARY.Bandwidth: How many bytes can move per second; distinct from memory capacity.
GLOSSARY.Batch invariance: A supported guarantee that changing co-batch membership does not change a request’s result.
GLOSSARY.BF16 / FP16: Two-byte floating-point formats with different precision/range tradeoffs.
GLOSSARY.Checkpoint: Saved model parameters/configuration at a particular point; may be full weights or only an adapter.
GLOSSARY.Collective: A coordinated communication operation among device ranks, such as all-reduce.
GLOSSARY.CP: Context parallelism: divide sequence work among devices.
GLOSSARY.CUDA graph: A captured device-work graph reused to reduce launch overhead, under shape and memory constraints.
GLOSSARY.Decode: Iteratively extend a sequence using retained model state.
GLOSSARY.DP: Data parallelism: split independent work, with details depending on the layer/system.
GLOSSARY.EPLB: Expert-parallel load balancing: place/map expert work to reduce skew.
GLOSSARY.EP: Expert parallelism: distribute expert ownership across devices.
GLOSSARY.EOS: End-of-sequence marker or corresponding termination condition.
GLOSSARY.FLOP: One floating-point arithmetic operation; FLOP/s measures a rate.
GLOSSARY.GEMM: General matrix multiplication, a central building block of model execution.
GLOSSARY.GQA: Grouped-query attention: query heads share fewer KV heads.
GLOSSARY.HBM: High-bandwidth accelerator memory; capacity and transfer bandwidth are separate limits.
GLOSSARY.Kernel: A device program implementing one or more numerical operations.
GLOSSARY.KV cache: Retained keys and values or compatible attention state for preceding tokens.
GLOSSARY.LoRA: Low-rank adaptation: a compact parameter update to selected base-model matrices.
GLOSSARY.MLA: Multi-head latent attention: compressed attention representations; not a paging scheme.
GLOSSARY.MoE: Mixture of experts: selectively activate expert networks for each token.
GLOSSARY.Oracle: A reference computation or criterion that decides whether a property holds.
GLOSSARY.P99: The value at or below which 99% of measured samples fall; state the sampling boundary.
GLOSSARY.Prefill: Process known input tokens and build attention state.
GLOSSARY.Rank: One participant in a distributed process group.
GLOSSARY.RoPE: Rotary positional embeddings: a positional transformation of attention representations.
GLOSSARY.SLO: Service-level objective: a measurable target such as a latency percentile.
GLOSSARY.Softmax: Convert arbitrary scores to nonnegative probabilities summing to one.
GLOSSARY.SWA: Sliding-window attention: limit directly visible local key positions.
GLOSSARY.Teacher forcing: Feed a known continuation to compare model predictions on identical prefixes.
GLOSSARY.Tensor: A multidimensional array of numerical values.
GLOSSARY.TP: Tensor parallelism: split an operation/tensor across devices.
GLOSSARY.TTFT / ITL: Time to first token / inter-token latency. Specify queueing and delivery boundaries.
GLOSSARY.Weights: Learned numerical parameters defining the model’s calculations.

What this is built on.

The learning choices

Recall plus worked practice

Try a solution step before revealing it, then practice both recall and new scenarios. This draws on retrieval research and mnemonic-medium design; it does not imply this course has been experimentally validated.

Retrieval inside worked examples (2025) ↗How Might We Learn? ↗

Assistance is not mastery

Hints, example solutions and AI grades help practice. First attempts, later unassisted explanations and runnable checks provide different evidence. Learning studies in math and physics are informative but do not establish outcomes for GPU engineering.

placement.prompt: A model is generating token 501. Why can it reuse the keys and values it computed for the first 500 positions instead of recomputing them?
options: A token's key and value depend only on which token it is, so they are the same in every sentence.
Each position attends only to itself and earlier ones, so later tokens cannot change them.
The weights are frozen during inference, and fixed weights alone make every saved vector permanent.
placement.why: Causal masking means an earlier position never reads later tokens, so its hidden states, keys and values are final once computed. Keys and values do depend on context and position, and frozen weights would not be enough if earlier positions could attend forward.

placement.prompt: Two engines run the same weights with greedy decoding. They agree for 19 tokens and pick different 20th tokens. At that step the reference's top two logits differ by 0.001. What is the most reasonable first reading?
options: One engine's KV cache must be corrupt, since a correct engine reproduces greedy output exactly.
Greedy decoding samples at random among the top tokens, so occasional divergence is expected.
Different arithmetic order can round the logits differently and flip a near tie.
placement.why: Low-precision sums computed in a different order give slightly different results, and a 0.001 gap is within that noise. Greedy decoding is deterministic given the logits, and a cache bug would usually show up as larger logit differences on teacher-forced prefixes.

placement.prompt: On one GPU, a decode step for 32 requests takes far less than 32 times as long as a decode step for one request. What mainly explains this?
options: Each step reads the weights from memory once and applies them to all 32 tokens.
The 32 requests share one KV cache, so attention is computed only once per step.
Only one of the 32 requests produces a token per step, in rotation.
placement.why: Small-batch decoding is limited by moving weights from memory, and a batch spreads that one read over many tokens. Each request still keeps its own KV cache, and every request in the batch gets a token each step.

placement.prompt: A paged KV cache uses pages of 16 token positions. Someone proposes pages of 256 positions. Which trade-off should you expect?
options: Larger pages give more prefix-cache hits because each page covers more shared text.
Less bookkeeping, but more unused slots per last page and coarser prefix sharing.
No memory change, because paging only renames positions and never wastes any slots.
placement.why: A request's final page is usually only partly filled, so bigger pages waste more memory per request, and prefix reuse that works in whole pages can only share complete pages. Fewer, larger pages do reduce metadata and indirection, which is why page size is tuned rather than maximized.

placement.prompt: In an expert-parallel mixture-of-experts layer, a token's router picks experts that live on other GPUs. What has to happen for that token?
options: Every GPU first receives a full copy of the chosen experts' weights for that layer.
Nothing crosses GPUs, because each GPU runs its own tokens through its local experts only.
Its activations go to the GPUs owning those experts, and the outputs come back.
placement.why: Expert parallelism moves tokens to the experts, not weights to the tokens: a dispatch sends activations to the owning ranks and a combine step gathers the weighted results. That exchange is also why one overloaded rank can hold up the rest.

placement.prompt: A team raises the maximum speculative draft length from 3 to 8 tokens. When is that most likely to slow decoding down?
options: When batches are large: extra positions cost compute and later drafts rarely survive.
Never, because the target model checks every draft position in one pass at no extra cost.
Whenever drafts are rejected, because a rejection changes the target model's output distribution.
placement.why: Acceptance compounds, so the sixth to eighth draft positions survive rarely, and once a large batch makes the target compute-bound, verifying them is no longer nearly free. Exact verification keeps the target distribution whatever the acceptance rate, so rejection costs time rather than correctness.

placement.prompt: A LoRA adapter trained on base revision R1 loads onto base revision R2 with no shape errors. What does the clean load establish?
options: That the adapted model behaves as trained, since a LoRA update does not depend on the base values.
Only that names and shapes matched; R2's weight values may not be the ones it was trained on.
Nothing at all, because LoRA loaders skip shape and name checks entirely and accept any file.
placement.why: An adapter is a learned correction to specific base weights, so it is only the trained model on top of those weights. Two revisions of one architecture share shapes but not values, so behavior has to be compared against the trained reference.

placement.prompt: Five repeated runs of the baseline measure 950 to 1,080 tokens/s. A change scores 1,100 tokens/s in a single run. What can you conclude?
options: That the change is a regression, since the baseline sometimes reaches 1,080.
That the change gives about a 10% gain, since it was the only difference.
Not yet; repeat the change as often as the baseline and compare.
placement.why: One run of the change sits just above a baseline that varies by about 13%, so the gain could be noise. Repeating both configurations under the same workload shows whether their ranges actually separate.
